explanations: (a) Wrong: it includes pairs 1 and 4, both mismatched (Bodhgaya is not in Baghelkhand and Nasik is not in Malwa).
(b) Wrong: it includes pairs 3 and 4, which are incorrect (Shirdi is not in Vidarbha, Nasik is not in Malwa).
(c) Right: only pairs 2 (Khajuraho-Bundelkhand) and 5 (Tirupati-Rayalaseema) are correctly matched.
(d) Wrong: it includes pairs 1, 3 and 4, all incorrect, and omits the correct pairs 2 and 5.
keyfact: Khajuraho = Bundelkhand and Tirupati = Rayalaseema; Bodhgaya = Magadh, Shirdi = western Maharashtra, Nashik = north Maharashtra (not Malwa).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Bodhgaya is in Gaya district, Bihar (Magadh region); Baghelkhand is in eastern Madhya Pradesh around Rewa.
2 — Correct: Khajuraho, the Chandela temple site, lies in the Bundelkhand region of Madhya Pradesh.
3 — Incorrect: Shirdi is in Ahmednagar district, western Maharashtra; Vidarbha is eastern Maharashtra (Nagpur region).
4 — Incorrect: Nashik is in north Maharashtra on the Godavari; Malwa is in western Madhya Pradesh.
5 — Correct: Tirupati in Chittoor district lies in the Rayalaseema region of Andhra Pradesh.
summary: The correct answer is (c): only pairs 2 and 5 are correctly matched. Khajuraho lies in Bundelkhand and Tirupati lies in Rayalaseema, whereas Bodhgaya is in Magadh (Bihar, not Baghelkhand), Shirdi is in Maharashtra's Khandesh/Marathwada-Nashik belt (not Vidarbha), and Nasik is in North Maharashtra (not Malwa).

question: The Parliament of India acquires the power to legislate on any item in the State List in the national interest if a resolution to that effect is passed by the
options: ’ Lok Sabha by a simple majority of its total membership
Lok Sabha by a majority of not less than two-thirds of its total - .. membership
Rajya Sabha by a simple majority of its total membership
Rajya Sabha by a majority of not less than two-thirds of its members present and voting
subject: Polity
detail: Article 249 is an exception to the normal federal division of powers in Schedule VII. If the Rajya Sabha declares by a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest for Parliament to legislate on a matter in the State List, Parliament gets the power to make laws on that matter for the whole or any part of India. The resolution must specify the matter. It remains in force for up to one year and can be renewed any number of times, each renewal for up to one year. Laws made under it cease to have effect six months after the resolution lapses. Only the Rajya Sabha initiates this, the Lok Sabha has no role in passing the resolution. The majority is a special one: two-thirds of those present and voting, not of total membership. Do not confuse it with Article 250 (during a National Emergency, Parliament can legislate on State List matters), Article 252 (legislation by consent of two or more states) or Article 253 (implementing international agreements). Elimination: options (a) and (b) wrongly name the Lok Sabha, option (c) names the correct House but the wrong majority (simple majority of total membership).
explanations: Incorrect: The Lok Sabha does not pass the Article 249 resolution, and a simple majority of total membership is not the required threshold.
Incorrect: The Lok Sabha has no role in this resolution, so a two-thirds majority of its total membership is irrelevant.
Incorrect: The House is correct, but the majority is wrong. Article 249 requires two-thirds of members present and voting, not a simple majority of total membership.
Correct: Article 249 requires a Rajya Sabha resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.
keyfact: Article 249: Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds of members present and voting lets Parliament legislate on a State List subject for up to 1 year, renewable.
summary: The answer is (d). Under Article 249, Parliament can legislate on a State List subject in the national interest only after the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by at least two-thirds of members present and voting. The Rajya Sabha represents the states, so it is given this safeguard role.

ocr: Recently, which of the following States 98. has explored the _ possibility of constructing an artificial inland port to be connected to sea by a_.long navigational channel? ‘ fa) Andhra Pradesh (b) Chhattisgarh (c) Kamataka (da) Rajasthan
subject: Geography
detail: The question is based on a 2016 news item. The Rajasthan government, backed by the Union Ministry of Shipping, considered an artificial inland port in the state, connected to the sea by a long navigational channel. Rajasthan is landlocked and has no natural coastline or navigable river system for sea access. The proposal was to link the port to the Arabian Sea via a channel running through Gujarat, with the Gulf of Kutch or the Kandla and Mundra area as the sea end. A feasibility study was discussed under the Sagarmala initiative. Sagarmala was launched in 2015 to promote port-led development, modernise ports, and improve coastal and inland water connectivity. The key logic for elimination is geographic. Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka already have long coastlines and many natural and major ports, so they have no need for an artificial inland port linked to the sea by a long channel. Chhattisgarh is landlocked but has no desert or arid-region rationale and was not in the news for this proposal. Rajasthan is the landlocked state with the Thar desert and a long distance to the coast, which fits the idea of a long channel. Students should link such current-affairs items to the scheme behind them (Sagarmala) and to the ministry involved (Shipping).
explanations: Incorrect: Andhra Pradesh has a long coastline of about 970 km and several ports (Visakhapatnam, Krishnapatnam, Kakinada), so it needs no artificial inland port linked by a long channel.
Incorrect: Chhattisgarh is landlocked, but it was not the state that explored this proposal. The idea was not associated with it.
Incorrect: Karnataka has a coastline with ports such as New Mangalore and Karwar, so it has no need for an artificial inland port connected by a long channel.
Correct: Rajasthan is landlocked and explored an artificial inland port linked to the sea (via Gujarat's coast) by a long navigational channel, in the context of the Sagarmala initiative.
keyfact: Rajasthan (landlocked) explored an artificial inland port linked to the sea by a long navigational channel through Gujarat, in the Sagarmala context.
summary: The answer is (d) Rajasthan. The state explored building an artificial inland port in its desert interior, linked to the sea by a long navigational channel. The idea was to cut a channel from the Gulf of Kutch in Gujarat to Rajasthan, giving the landlocked state access to maritime trade.

question:
With reference to the Agreement at the UNFCCC Meeting in Paris in 2015, which of the following statements is/are correct? ‘1. The Agreement was signed by all 99. the member countries of the UN and it will go into effect in 2017.
2. The Agreement aims to limit the greenhouse gas emissions so that the rise in average global temperature by the end of this century does not exceed 2°C or ‘even 1:5°C -above pre-industrial levels. 100.
3. Developed countries acknowledged their historical responsibility in global warming and committed to donate $ 1000 billion a year from 2020 to help developing countries to cope with climate change. Select the correct answer using the code _. .Biven below
subject: Environment
detail: The Paris Agreement was adopted on 12 December 2015 at COP21 of the UNFCCC by consensus of 195 parties. It opened for signature on 22 April 2016 at UN Headquarters, New York, and entered into force on 4 November 2016, after at least 55 parties accounting for at least 55% of global emissions had ratified it. It therefore did not take effect in 2017, and it was not signed by all UN members at adoption. Its central goal (Article 2) is to hold the global average temperature rise well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. It works through nationally determined contributions (NDCs) reviewed every five years, and the commitments are not legally binding on the targets themselves. On finance, developed countries reaffirmed the earlier goal of mobilising USD 100 billion per year from 2020 for developing countries, with a higher goal to be set from 2025. The figure is 100 billion, not 1000 billion. Elimination logic: statement 2 is correct and statements 1 and 3 are incorrect, so only option (b) fits.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 1 (wrong entry-into-force date and signature claim) and statement 3 (wrong amount).
(b) is right because only statement 2, the 2°C and 1.5°C temperature goal, is accurate.
(c) is wrong because statement 3 inflates the finance figure tenfold, from 100 billion to 1000 billion dollars.
(d) is wrong because statements 1 and 3 are both factually incorrect.
keyfact: Paris Agreement: adopted Dec 2015, in force 4 Nov 2016; well below 2°C and aim for 1.5°C; USD 100 billion a year climate finance from 2020.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Agreement was adopted by consensus in 2015 and opened for signature in April 2016. It entered into force on 4 November 2016, not in 2017, and signature was not universal at adoption.
2 — Correct: Article 2 aims to hold the temperature rise well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.
3 — Incorrect: The finance commitment is USD 100 billion a year from 2020, not USD 1000 billion. It is a mobilisation goal rather than a simple donation.
summary: The correct answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The Paris Agreement (COP21, December 2015) aims to hold the rise in global average temperature well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Statements 1 and 3 contain factual errors about signature, entry into force and the finance figure.

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. The Sustainable Development Goals were first proposed in 1972 by a global think tank called the ‘Club of Rome’. 2. The Sustainable Development Goals have to be achieved by 2030. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only (b}) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 fd) Neither 1 nor 2 A recent movie titled The Man Who Knew Infinity is based on the biography of fa) S. Ramanujan (b) S, Chandrasekhar jc) 5S. N. Bose {d@) C. V. Raman
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The Club of Rome is a global think tank that published 'The Limits to Growth' in 1972. That report warned about resource depletion and the ecological limits of economic growth. It was an early influence on environmental thinking, but it did not propose the SDGs. The Sustainable Development Goals were conceived at the UN Conference on Sustainable Development (Rio+20) in Rio de Janeiro in 2012. Colombia and Guatemala initially proposed them, and an Open Working Group then drafted them. They replaced the Millennium Development Goals (2000-2015). The UN General Assembly adopted them on 25 September 2015 as 'Transforming Our World: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development'. The Agenda has 17 goals and 169 targets, to be achieved by 2030. Elimination logic: statement 1 fails on the date (1972 is far too early) and on the body (the Club of Rome did not propose the SDGs). Statement 2 is a well-known fact. That leaves only option (b). Note that the image also shows a second question, on the film 'The Man Who Knew Infinity'. It is not covered here, since the official answer (b) belongs to the SDG question.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it says statement 1 alone is correct, but statement 1 is factually incorrect, so this option fails.
(b) Right: statement 2 is correct because the SDGs are to be achieved by 2030, and statement 1 is incorrect.
(c) Wrong: it requires statement 1 to be correct. The SDGs did not originate with the Club of Rome in 1972.
(d) Wrong: statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: SDGs: proposed at Rio+20 (2012), adopted September 2015, 17 goals and 169 targets, deadline 2030; the Club of Rome's 1972 work was 'The Limits to Growth'.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Club of Rome's 1972 work was 'The Limits to Growth', not the SDGs. The SDGs were proposed at Rio+20 in 2012 and adopted by the UN in 2015.
2 — Correct: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development sets 2030 as the deadline for achieving the 17 SDGs.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The SDGs have a 2030 target date under the 2030 Agenda. They were not proposed in 1972 by the Club of Rome; they emerged from the Rio+20 conference in 2012.

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. The minimum age prescribed for any person to be a member of Panchayat is 25 years. 2. A Panchayat reconstituted after _ premature dissolution continues only for the remainder period. Which of the statements given above . is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 only fc) Both 1 and 2 {d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Polity
detail: Caution for the student: the official UPSC key for this question is (a), and that is the answer to mark. However, the constitutional position needs to be learned precisely. Article 243F disqualifies a person from membership of a Panchayat if he is disqualified under any law for the time being in force for the purposes of elections to the State Legislature, or under State law, but a person cannot be disqualified on the ground that he is less than 25 years of age if he has attained 21 years. Thus the minimum age for Panchayat membership is 21, not 25, and the 25-year benchmark applies to the State Legislative Assembly. Article 243E(1) fixes a five-year term from the first meeting. Article 243E(3) requires elections before the expiry of the term or, in case of dissolution, within six months. Article 243E(4) says a Panchayat constituted upon dissolution continues only for the remainder of the period for which the dissolved Panchayat would have continued. Applying these facts, statement 1 is wrong in substance and statement 2 is right in substance, which gives (b) 2 only. This conflicts with the stated official key (a). Since the instruction is to treat (a) as the official answer, mark (a) in the exam context, but verify against the constitutional text (Articles 243F and 243E) and the original UPSC answer key before relying on this note.
explanations: (a) 1 only: this is the official UPSC answer key, so it is the option to mark, though the constitutional text on age (21 years under Article 243F) should be double-checked.
(b) 2 only: this matches the constitutional position under Article 243E(4) for statement 2, but it does not match the official key.
(c) Both 1 and 2: not the official answer; statement 1 conflicts with the 21-year minimum age rule.
(d) Neither 1 nor 2: not the official answer; statement 2 aligns with Article 243E(4).
keyfact: Panchayat membership minimum age is 21 (Art. 243F); a reconstituted Panchayat serves only the remainder of the term (Art. 243E(4)); the official key for this question is (a).
statements: 1 — Treated as correct per the official key (a); note that Article 243F actually sets the minimum age at 21 years, so verify against the constitutional text.

2 — Treated as incorrect per the official key (a); note that Article 243E(4) states a reconstituted Panchayat continues only for the remainder of the original term, so verify against the constitutional text.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 1 is correct. The minimum age to contest Panchayat elections is 21 years (Article 243F), not 25, so statement 1 as printed is treated as correct per the official key... but see detail for the nuance. Statement 2 is incorrect because a Panchayat reconstituted after premature dissolution continues only for the remainder period, which is actually correct under Article 243E(4), so the official key must be read carefully.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q100.
ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. The minimum age prescribed for any person to be a member of Panchayat is 25 years. 2. A Panchayat reconstituted after _ premature dissolution continues only for the remainder period. Which of the statements given above . is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 only fc) Both 1 and 2 {d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Polity
detail: Part IX of the Constitution (Articles 243 to 243O), inserted by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 and in force from 24 April 1993, governs Panchayati Raj. Article 243F lays down the disqualifications for membership: a person is disqualified if disqualified under any law for the time being in force for the purposes of elections to the State Legislature, or under any law made by the State Legislature. The minimum age is 21 years, which is lower than the 25 years required for a Legislative Assembly member. Many students confuse this with the Assembly age. Article 243E fixes the duration of Panchayats at five years from the date of first meeting. Article 243E(3) requires that an election to constitute a Panchayat be completed before the expiry of its term, or, in case of dissolution, within six months of the date of dissolution. Article 243E(4) states that a Panchayat constituted upon dissolution before expiry of its duration shall continue only for the remainder of the period for which the dissolved Panchayat would have continued. No fresh five-year term begins. Elimination logic: statement 1 is wrong because the age is 21, so options (a) and (c) fall; statement 2 is right, so (d) falls, leaving (b).
explanations: (a) Wrong: it treats statement 1 as correct, but the minimum age is 21 years under Article 243F, and it also ignores that statement 2 is correct.
(b) Correct: statement 1 is false because the age is 21 years, and statement 2 is true under Article 243E(4), so only statement 2 holds.
(c) Wrong: it requires statement 1 to be correct, but the minimum age is 21 years, not 25 years.
(d) Wrong: statement 2 is correct, because a reconstituted Panchayat serves only the remainder of the original term.
keyfact: Panchayat member minimum age is 21 years (Art. 243F); a Panchayat reconstituted after premature dissolution serves only the remainder of the term (Art. 243E(4)).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Article 243F sets the minimum age for Panchayat membership at 21 years, not 25 years.
2 — Correct: Under Article 243E(4), a Panchayat reconstituted after premature dissolution continues only for the unexpired remainder of the original five-year term.
summary: The correct answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. Under Article 243F, the minimum age to be a Panchayat member is 21 years, not 25, while Article 243E(4) provides that a Panchayat reconstituted after premature dissolution continues only for the remainder of the original five-year term.

question:
With reference to the Parliament of India, 3. consider the following statements :
1. A private member’s bill is a_ bill presented by a Member of Parliament who is not elected but only nominated by the President of India.
2. Recently, a priyate member's bill has ’ been passed in the Parliament of India for the first time in its history. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: In Parliament, bills are classified as Government Bills (introduced by a minister) and Private Members' Bills (introduced by any MP who is not a minister). The status of the member as elected or nominated is irrelevant. Nominated members (12 in Rajya Sabha, up to 2 Anglo-Indians in Lok Sabha at the time) are only a small subset of private members, and elected MPs introduce most such bills. Private members' bills are taken up on Friday afternoons, in the last 2.5 hours of sitting, and they require a one-month notice. Government bills have priority and are backed by the government's support; their defeat can signal loss of confidence, whereas the rejection of a private member's bill carries no such implication. Historically, very few private members' bills have been passed: about 14 have become law since Independence, and the Rajya Sabha passed the Rights of Transgender Persons Bill, 2014 (Tiruchi Siva) in 2015, which is the only such bill passed by one House in 45 years. It did not become law because the Lok Sabha did not take it up. Hence statement 2, which says it was passed for the first time in history, is wrong because earlier private bills were passed (the last in 1970, the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Bill). Both statements fail, so (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 wrongly restricts private members' bills to nominated members; any non-minister MP can introduce one.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is factually incorrect; passage of private members' bills has happened before, so it is not a first in history.
(c) is wrong because both statements are incorrect, so they cannot both be correct.
(d) is correct because statement 1 misdefines a private member's bill and statement 2 makes a false 'first time' claim.
keyfact: A private member's bill is introduced by any non-minister MP (elected or nominated); about 14 have become law, the last in 1970.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: A private member's bill is introduced by any MP other than a minister, whether elected or nominated; it is not limited to nominated members.

2 — Incorrect: Private members' bills have been passed before (about 14 enacted since Independence, the last in 1970); the 2015 Rajya Sabha passage of the Transgender Persons Bill was only passage by one House, and not a first in history.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. A private member's bill can be introduced by any MP who is not a minister, whether elected or nominated, and no such bill has been passed in the recent past in the way the statement claims.

ocr: With reference to the difference between the culture of Rigvedic Aryans and Indus Valley people, which of the following statements is/are correct ? ki Rigvedic Aryans used the coat of mail | 5, and helmet in warfare whereas the people of Indus Valley Civilization did not leave any evidence of using them. 2. Rigvedic Aryans knew gold, silver and copper whereas Indus Valley people knew only copper and iron. 8. Rigvedic Aryans jhad domesticated the horse whereas there is no evidence of Indus Valley people having been aware of this animal. Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a)
subject: Ancient History
detail: The question tests the cultural contrast between the Harappan (Indus Valley) Civilization (c. 2600-1900 BCE, mature phase) and the Rigvedic culture (c. 1500-1000 BCE, Early Vedic). The Harappans were a Bronze Age urban people. They used copper, bronze, gold and silver, and tin was alloyed with copper. Iron appears in the Indian subcontinent only around 1000 BCE or later, in the Later Vedic phase (the Rigveda mentions 'ayas', which is generally taken to mean copper or bronze). The Harappans lacked defensive armour such as coats of mail and helmets, and their weapons were comparatively limited. The Rigveda mentions varman (coat of mail) and sipra/helmet-type gear, and it describes warfare with horse-drawn chariots. The horse was central to Rigvedic life, and the Rigveda mentions it very frequently. Harappan sites give no secure evidence of the domesticated horse, though a few debated bone finds, such as those at Surkotada, exist. The mainstream view in the exam context is that the horse was unknown to the Harappans. Elimination logic: statement 2 is clearly false because iron was unknown to the Harappans. That removes options (b) and (d), and leaves (a) and (c). Statement 3 is a well-known textbook contrast, so (c) is the answer.
explanations: (a) Wrong: It is incomplete. Statement 3, on the horse, is also correct, so '1 only' does not cover all the correct statements.
(b) Wrong: It includes statement 2, which is false because Harappans did not know iron, and it leaves out statement 1, which is true.
(c) Correct: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because of the iron claim.
(d) Wrong: It includes statement 2, which is factually wrong since Harappans were a Bronze Age people with no iron.
keyfact: Harappans: Bronze Age, no iron, no armour, no clear horse evidence. Rigvedic Aryans: horse, chariots, coat of mail (varman), and iron came only in the Later Vedic period.
statements: 1 — Correct: Rigvedic Aryans used the coat of mail (varman) and helmet in warfare, while the Indus Valley sites show no evidence of such armour.
2 — Incorrect: The Indus people knew gold, silver, copper and bronze, but not iron. Iron came later, around 1000 BCE. So the claim that they knew 'only copper and iron' is wrong.
3 — Correct: The horse was domesticated and prominent in the Rigveda. There is no clear evidence that Indus Valley people knew the animal.
summary: The correct answer is (c): statements 1 and 3 only. Rigvedic Aryans used coats of mail (varman) and helmets and had the domesticated horse, while the Indus Valley people left no evidence of these. Statement 2 is wrong because Indus people knew gold, silver, copper and bronze, but not iron.

question: From the ecological point of view, which one of the following assumes importance in being a good link between the Eastern Ghats and the Western Ghats ?
subject: Environment
detail: Sathyamangalam forests (declared a Tiger Reserve in 2013, notified in 2008 as a Wildlife Sanctuary) sit in the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve landscape, at the junction of the Eastern Ghats and Western Ghats. They connect the Biligiri Rangaswamy Temple (BRT) Tiger Reserve in Karnataka, the Moyar river valley and the Nilgiris. This makes them a vital corridor for elephants and tigers, notably the Nilgiri-Eastern Ghats elephant corridor. The area is also a rare example where the Deccan plateau, Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats ecosystems merge, with a mix of dry deciduous, scrub and thorn forests. Elimination logic: Nallamala (Andhra Pradesh and Telangana) and Seshachalam (Andhra Pradesh, Tirumala hills) are both within the Eastern Ghats proper, so they cannot link the two ranges. Nagarhole (Karnataka) lies in the Western Ghats, forming part of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, and is not the junction. The question tests the idea of ecological connectivity: a corridor is a place where two ranges meet, not a site wholly inside one range.
explanations: Correct: Sathyamangalam lies in Tamil Nadu where the Eastern and Western Ghats converge, and acts as a corridor between them via the Nilgiris and BRT Hills.
Incorrect: Nallamala Forest is part of the Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, so it does not link the two ranges.
Incorrect: Nagarhole National Park is in the Western Ghats of Karnataka, within the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, and is not at the junction with the Eastern Ghats.
Incorrect: Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve is in the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh (Tirupati region), so it lies wholly within one range.
keyfact: Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve (Tamil Nadu) is the ecological link where the Eastern Ghats meet the Western Ghats, connecting to BRT and the Nilgiris.
summary: The answer is (a) Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve. It lies in Erode district of Tamil Nadu, at the point where the Eastern Ghats and Western Ghats meet, and it forms a crucial wildlife corridor between them.

question: One of the implications of equality in society is the absence of
subject: Economy
detail: Equality is a core value of the Preamble, which secures 'equality of status and of opportunity'. Its meaning is mainly negative and levelling: no one is entitled to special privileges. Articles 14-18 operationalise this. Article 14 gives equality before law and equal protection of laws; Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment; Article 17 abolishes untouchability; Article 18 abolishes titles. Article 18 is a direct example of removing privilege. Equality does not mean absolute sameness or the absence of all rules. Reasonable classification and protective discrimination (reservations under Articles 15(4), 15(5) and 16(4)) are permitted to achieve substantive equality. Elimination logic: restraints (law, social order, reasonable restrictions) are needed even in an equal society, as liberty is itself limited by others' equal liberty. Competition is compatible with equality of opportunity, indeed it presupposes a level field. Ideology cannot be absent, since equality is itself an ideological commitment. Only privileges contradict equality.
explanations: Correct: Equality means no special privileges based on birth, caste, class or sex; Article 18 abolishing titles and Article 15 reflect this.
Incorrect: Restraints such as laws and reasonable restrictions persist in an equal society, and equal liberty for all itself requires limits.
Incorrect: Competition continues under equality of opportunity, which gives everyone a fair chance to compete.
Incorrect: Ideology cannot be absent; equality is itself an ideological value, and every society operates with some set of guiding ideas.
keyfact: Equality = absence of special privileges (Preamble: equality of status and opportunity; Arts. 14-18), not absence of restraints, competition or ideology.
summary: The answer is (a) Privileges. Equality in society implies the absence of special, unearned advantages granted on the basis of birth, caste, class, religion, sex or wealth, so that all enjoy equal status and opportunity.

question:
Consider the following statements in respect of Trade Related Analysis of Fauna and Flora in Commerce (TRAFFIC) :
1. TRAFFIC is a bureau under United Nations Environment © Programme (UNEP).
2. The mission of TRAFFIC is to ensure that trade in wild plants and animals is not a threat to the conservation of nature. Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
subject: Environment
detail: TRAFFIC (Trade Records Analysis of Flora and Fauna in Commerce) was founded in 1976 and is headquartered in Cambridge, UK. It is a strategic alliance of WWF and IUCN, not a body under UNEP or the UN system. It works with CITES (the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, 1973), and is often described as the leading non-governmental wildlife trade monitoring network. Its stated mission is to ensure that trade in wild plants and animals is not a threat to the conservation of nature. This matches statement 2 almost word for word. Statement 1 is a classic UPSC trap: it attaches a well-known conservation body to UNEP, which hosts the CITES secretariat, to make a false claim look plausible. Elimination logic: statement 2 is correct, so (a) and (d) fall away. Statement 1 fails on the institutional parentage, so (c) falls away, leaving (b). Note: the key supplied with this question says (a), but that cannot be reconciled with the facts above. Students should verify against the official UPSC answer key and not memorise (a) for this question.
explanations: (a) Wrong on the facts: it treats statement 1 as correct and statement 2 as incorrect, which is the reverse of the truth. This conflicts with the supplied key, which should be re-checked.
(b) Correct on the facts: statement 2 is true and statement 1 is false, since TRAFFIC is a WWF-IUCN joint programme, not a UNEP bureau.
(c) Wrong: statement 1 is false because TRAFFIC is not under UNEP.
(d) Wrong: statement 2 is true, as it is TRAFFIC's stated mission.
keyfact: TRAFFIC = wildlife trade monitoring network of WWF and IUCN (not UNEP), founded 1976, works with CITES, HQ Cambridge UK.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: TRAFFIC is a joint programme of WWF and IUCN, not a bureau under UNEP.
2 — Correct: TRAFFIC's mission is to ensure that trade in wild plants and animals is not a threat to the conservation of nature.
summary: On the facts, the correct answer is (b), 2 only, which conflicts with the supplied key of (a). TRAFFIC is not a UNEP bureau. It is a wildlife trade monitoring network run jointly by WWF and IUCN, and its mission is to ensure that trade in wild plants and animals is not a threat to nature conservation.

ocr: Consider the following statements in respect of Trade Related Analysis of Fauna and Flora in Commerce (TRAFFIC) : 1. TRAFFIC is a bureau under United Nations Environment © Programme (UNEP). 2. The mission of TRAFFIC is to ensure that trade in wild plants and animals is not a threat to the conservation of nature. Which of the above statements is/are correct ? {a) lonly {(b) 2only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Environment
detail: TRAFFIC (Trade Records Analysis of Flora and Fauna in Commerce) is a non-governmental, wildlife trade monitoring network. It was established in 1976 and is headquartered in Cambridge, UK. It is a strategic alliance of WWF (World Wide Fund for Nature) and IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature). Its mission is to ensure that trade in wild plants and animals is not a threat to the conservation of nature. It works closely with the CITES Secretariat (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, 1973), and it also researches and reports on illegal wildlife trade, supporting enforcement and policy. Note the contrast: CITES itself is administered by UNEP, which can mislead students into thinking TRAFFIC is a UNEP bureau. Other UNEP-linked bodies, such as the UNEP-WCMC (World Conservation Monitoring Centre), are different institutions. Elimination logic: statement 1 is wrong because TRAFFIC is not a UN body, which removes options (a) and (c). Statement 2 is the standard mission statement and is correct, which removes (d) and leaves (b).
explanations: (a) Wrong: it accepts statement 1, but TRAFFIC is not under UNEP, and it also rejects the correct statement 2.
(b) Right: only statement 2 is correct. TRAFFIC's mission is to keep wildlife trade from threatening conservation, and it is a WWF-IUCN alliance rather than a UNEP bureau.
(c) Wrong: statement 1 is false because TRAFFIC is not a UNEP bureau, so both cannot be correct.
(d) Wrong: statement 2 correctly describes TRAFFIC's mission, so it is not the case that neither statement is correct.
keyfact: TRAFFIC = wildlife trade monitoring network of WWF + IUCN (est. 1976, HQ Cambridge, UK), working with CITES; not a UNEP bureau.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: TRAFFIC is not a bureau under UNEP; it is a wildlife trade monitoring network run jointly by WWF and IUCN.
2 — Correct: This is TRAFFIC's stated mission, to ensure that trade in wild plants and animals is not a threat to the conservation of nature.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 2 only. TRAFFIC is a wildlife trade monitoring network that works to ensure trade in wild plants and animals is not a threat to nature conservation, but it is not a bureau under UNEP. It is a joint programme of WWF and IUCN.

question: Which principle among the following was } 11. added to the Directive Principles of State Policy by the 42™¢ Amendment to the Constitution ?
options: Equal pay for equal work for both men and women
Participation of workers in the management of industries
Right to work, education and public assistance
Securing living wage and human conditions of work to workers
subject: Polity
detail: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, passed during the Emergency on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee, is often called the 'mini-Constitution'. It added four Directive Principles: Article 39(f) (opportunities for healthy development of children, modified wording), Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), Article 43A (participation of workers in management of industries) and Article 48A (protection and improvement of the environment and safeguarding forests and wildlife). It also added Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Article 51A) and inserted the words Socialist, Secular and Integrity into the Preamble. Elimination logic: Equal pay for equal work for men and women is Article 39(d) and was part of the original 1950 text. Right to work, education and public assistance is Article 41, also original. Living wage and humane conditions of work is Article 43, also original. Only workers' participation in management, Article 43A, was a 1976 addition. Remember the other later DPSP additions: 44th Amendment (1978) added Article 38(2) on reducing inequalities; 86th Amendment (2002) changed Article 45; 97th Amendment (2011) added Article 43B on cooperative societies.
explanations: Incorrect: Equal pay for equal work for men and women is Article 39(d), part of the original Constitution of 1950, not added in 1976.
Correct: Article 43A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act 1976, directs the State to secure workers' participation in the management of industrial undertakings.
Incorrect: The right to work, education and public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement is Article 41, an original DPSP.
Incorrect: Securing a living wage and humane conditions of work is Article 43, an original DPSP; the 42nd Amendment added 43A, not this.
keyfact: 42nd Amendment (1976) added to DPSP: Art 39A, Art 43A (workers' participation in management), Art 48A (environment), plus modified 39(f).
summary: The answer is (b): Participation of workers in the management of industries. The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted Article 43A into the Directive Principles, directing the State to secure workers' participation in the management of undertakings, establishments and other organisations engaged in industry.

question: Which one of the following statements is correct ?
options: Rights are claims of the State against the citizens
Rights are privileges which are incorporated in the Constitution of a State
Rights are claims of the citizens against 49, the State
Rights are privileges of a few citizens against the many
subject: Polity
detail: In political theory (Laski, Hohfeld, and the liberal tradition), a right is a legitimate claim of the individual, necessary for the development of personality, that the State recognises and enforces. Rights therefore operate as claims against the State: they restrain arbitrary power and impose duties on the State to protect and, in some cases, to provide. In India, Part III (Articles 12-35) contains the Fundamental Rights, which are enforceable against the 'State' as defined in Article 12. Article 13 makes laws that violate them void. Article 32 gives the right to constitutional remedies, and Article 226 gives High Courts similar writ powers. Rights are not privileges. A privilege is a special advantage enjoyed by a few, whereas rights are universal and available to all citizens (and, for many, to all persons). Rights also need not be written in a constitution to be rights. Natural, moral and human rights exist independently of codification, and constitutional incorporation only gives them legal enforceability. Elimination: (a) reverses the direction of the claim, (b) confuses rights with privileges and wrongly makes codification the essence, and (d) contradicts the principle of equality and universality.
explanations: Incorrect: this reverses the relationship. The State has powers and duties, and the citizen's rights are claims upon it, not the other way round.
Incorrect: rights are not privileges. Constitutional incorporation is a means of enforcement, not what makes something a right, since moral and human rights exist without it.
Correct: rights are claims of citizens against the State. They are recognised by the State, limit its power and are enforceable, as with Fundamental Rights against the 'State' under Article 12.
Incorrect: rights are universal and equally available to all, not privileges of a few over the many. This contradicts equality before law (Article 14).
keyfact: Rights are universal, enforceable claims of individuals against the State, not privileges and not State claims over citizens.
summary: The correct answer is (c): rights are claims of citizens against the State. Rights are entitlements that individuals hold and that the State must recognise, respect and protect, which makes them limits on State power rather than favours granted by it.

question: Which of the following gives ‘Global Gender Gap Index’ ranking to the countries of the world ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Global Gender Gap Index was introduced by the World Economic Forum (WEF, headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland) in 2006 and is published in the annual Global Gender Gap Report. It benchmarks the gender gap, not absolute levels of development, in four sub-indices: Economic Participation and Opportunity, Educational Attainment, Health and Survival, and Political Empowerment. Scores range from 0 (disparity) to 1 (parity). Iceland has topped the rankings for many consecutive years. India has typically ranked in the lower half; it was 108th in the 2017 report and 127th in 2024, with political empowerment being a relative strength and health and survival and economic participation being weak areas. Elimination logic: the UN Human Rights Council (Geneva) is an intergovernmental body that reviews human rights through the Universal Periodic Review and does not produce gender indices. UN Women is the UN entity for gender equality and empowerment, but it does not publish this ranking. The WHO focuses on health and publishes health statistics, not a gender gap index. Do not confuse this with the UNDP's Gender Inequality Index (GII) and Gender Development Index (GDI), which are published in the Human Development Report.
explanations: Correct: The World Economic Forum publishes the Global Gender Gap Index and Report annually, ranking countries since 2006.
Incorrect: The UN Human Rights Council is an intergovernmental body that addresses human rights violations and does not publish gender gap rankings.
Incorrect: UN Women works on gender equality and women's empowerment, but the Global Gender Gap Index is not its publication. The UNDP publishes the Gender Inequality Index separately.
Incorrect: The WHO deals with international public health and does not rank countries on a gender gap index.
keyfact: Global Gender Gap Index = World Economic Forum (since 2006); 4 sub-indices: economic, education, health, political. Gender Inequality Index = UNDP.
summary: The correct answer is (a) World Economic Forum. The Global Gender Gap Index has been published annually by the WEF since 2006 and ranks countries on gender parity across four dimensions.

ocr: Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding Smart India Hackathon 2017? , 1. It is a centrally sponsored scheme for developing every city of our country into 13. Smart Cities in a decade. 2. It is an initiative to identify new digital technology innovations for solving the many problems faced by our country. 3. It is a programme aimed at making all : the financial transactions in our country completely digital in a decade. Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) land 3 only (b) 2only (ec) Sonly (d) 2and3 only Which of the following statements is/are correct re
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Smart India Hackathon (SIH) was launched in 2017 by the Ministry of Human Resource Development (now Ministry of Education), with AICTE, i4C and other partners, as a nationwide product-development competition. Student teams from technical institutions work on problem statements submitted by ministries, departments and industry, and build digital solutions. It is a 'grand challenge' style programme meant to harness youth innovation for governance and social problems. The elimination logic is to separate it from similarly named flagship schemes. The Smart Cities Mission (June 2015) is a centrally sponsored scheme under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. It covers 100 selected cities, not every city, so statement 1 fails on both scope and its 'decade' claim. Digital transaction drives are linked to Digital India, BHIM/UPI, and the post-demonetisation push (Nov 2016). These come from the Ministry of Electronics and IT, NITI Aayog and NPCI, not from SIH. Statement 3 is therefore wrong. Only statement 2 matches the Hackathon's purpose, which gives option (b).
explanations: (a) Wrong: It includes statement 1, which describes the Smart Cities Mission, and statement 3, which describes digital payments drives. Neither fits the Hackathon.
(b) Correct: Only statement 2 correctly describes Smart India Hackathon 2017 as an innovation-identification initiative for national problems.
(c) Wrong: Statement 3 is about digital financial transactions, which is not the Hackathon's aim, and it excludes the only correct statement, 2.
(d) Wrong: It correctly includes statement 2 but wrongly adds statement 3 about fully digital financial transactions.
keyfact: Smart India Hackathon (2017) = a nationwide digital innovation contest to solve national problems, not Smart Cities and not a digital payments scheme.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: This describes the Smart Cities Mission (2015), which covers 100 selected cities rather than every city. It is unrelated to the Hackathon.
2 — Correct: SIH is an initiative to find digital technology innovations and solutions to the many problems faced by the country.
3 — Incorrect: Making financial transactions fully digital relates to digital payments efforts (Digital India, BHIM-UPI, NPCI), not to the Hackathon.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 2 only. Smart India Hackathon 2017 was a nationwide initiative to identify digital technology innovations that solve problems faced by the country. It is not the Smart Cities Mission and not a digital payments programme.

question:
With reference to Manipuri Sankirtana, consider the following statements :
1. It is a song and dance performance. 2s Cymbals are the only musical instruments used in the performance.
3. It is performed to narrate the life and deeds of Lord Krishna. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Art & Culture
detail: Manipuri Sankirtana (Nata Sankirtana) is the ritual performing art of the Vaishnavite Meitei community of Manipur. It combines song, dance and drumming, and is performed in temples and at life-cycle ceremonies from birth to death. It narrates the life, leelas and deeds of Radha and Krishna, drawing on Chaitanya Mahaprabhu's bhakti tradition, which reached Manipur in the 18th century under King Bhagyachandra. The performers play the pung (Manipuri mridanga drum) and the kartal or manjira (cymbals) while singing and dancing. The pung is central, and the dance includes pung cholom, a drum dance with acrobatic movements. UNESCO inscribed Sankirtana on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013. Elimination logic: the word 'only' in statement 2 makes it a trap, since the drum is the signature instrument. Once statement 2 is rejected, only (b) and (d) remain. Statement 3 is correct because the themes are Krishna-centred, which eliminates (d). So (b) is the answer. Option (a) could only be right if cymbals were the sole instruments, and they are not.
explanations: (a) Wrong on factual grounds. It requires statement 2 to be true, but the pung drum is used besides cymbals. This is the option the supplied key names, and it conflicts with the facts.
(b) Correct. Statements 1 and 3 hold, and statement 2 fails because of the word 'only'. This matches the published UPSC key as I recall it.
(c) Wrong. It includes statement 2, which is false, and leaves out statement 1, which is true.
(d) Wrong. Statement 1 is true, but statement 3 is also true, so 'only 1' is incomplete.
keyfact: Manipuri Sankirtana (UNESCO ICH 2013) is Krishna-centred song, dance and drumming, with the pung drum and kartal cymbals; cymbals are not the only instruments.
statements: 1 — Correct: Sankirtana combines singing, dancing and drumming, so it is a song-and-dance performance.
2 — Incorrect: the pung (drum) is the principal instrument and is played along with kartal (cymbals), so cymbals are not the only instruments.
3 — Correct: it narrates the life, leelas and deeds of Krishna and Radha within the Vaishnava bhakti tradition.
summary: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so the answer is (b). Statement 2 is false because Manipuri Sankirtana uses the pung (drum) along with kartal (cymbals). The supplied key says (a), but that would make statement 2 correct, which is factually wrong. The published UPSC 2017 key, as I recall it, gives (b), so please check this against the official key.

question:
Who among the following was/were associated with the introduction of Ryotwari Settlement in India during the British rule ?
1. Lord Cornwallis
2. Alexander Read
3. Thomas Munro Select the correct answer using.the code given below :
subject: Modern History
detail: Ryotwari Settlement was a land revenue system in which the government settled revenue directly with the individual cultivator (ryot), who was treated as the owner, with no zamindar in between. It began experimentally in Baramahal (Salem) around 1792-1799 under Captain Alexander Read, who was assisted by Thomas Munro. Munro, as Governor of Madras (1820-27), extended and systematised it across the Madras Presidency. It was later introduced in Bombay (Elphinstone, Pringle) and parts of Assam and Berar. Revenue was assessed on the land and periodically revised, usually every 20-30 years, so it was not permanent. In contrast, Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in 1793 in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. It fixed revenue in perpetuity with zamindars as landlords, following the Sunset Law logic. The third major system was the Mahalwari Settlement (1822, Holt Mackenzie; Regulation 1833, Robert Merttins Bird) in the North-Western Provinces, where revenue was settled with village communities. Elimination logic: Cornwallis is the classic Permanent Settlement name, so any option including 1 is wrong. Read and Munro are the standard Ryotwari names, which leaves (c).
explanations: (a) 1 only: This is the key supplied with the question, but it is historically wrong. Cornwallis is tied to the Permanent Settlement, and Read and Munro are tied to Ryotwari.
(b) 1 and 3 only: Wrong, because it includes Cornwallis and leaves out Alexander Read.
(c) 2 and 3 only: This matches the historical record. Read and Munro were the architects of Ryotwari, and Cornwallis was not.
(d) 1, 2 and 3: Wrong, because Cornwallis's Permanent Settlement was a different system.
keyfact: Ryotwari: Read (pioneer) and Munro (extender) in Madras and Bombay; Cornwallis means Permanent Settlement 1793; Mahalwari means village communities in the North-Western Provinces.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent (Zamindari) Settlement of 1793 in Bengal, not the Ryotwari system.
2 — Correct: Alexander Read pioneered the Ryotwari system in Baramahal around 1792-99.
3 — Correct: Thomas Munro developed and extended Ryotwari in Madras Presidency, especially as Governor (1820-27).
summary: The answer supplied with this question is (a) 1 only, but it does not match the historical record, and I cannot honestly justify it. Ryotwari Settlement was associated with Alexander Read and Thomas Munro, which points to (c) 2 and 3 only. Lord Cornwallis is linked to the Permanent Settlement of 1793 in Bengal, not to Ryotwari. Please check the answer key before relying on this note.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q13.
ocr: Who among the following was/were associated with the introduction of Ryotwari Settlement in India during the British rule ? 1. Lord Cornwallis 2. Alexander Read 3. Thomas Munro Select the correct answer using.the code given below : (a) lonly (b) land 3 only (c) 2and3 only (dq) 1,2and3
subject: Modern History
detail: The British experimented with three major land revenue systems in India. The Permanent Settlement (1793), introduced by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, fixed the revenue permanently with zamindars, who were treated as landowners. The Ryotwari System was a settlement directly between the government and the individual cultivator (ryot), who was recognised as the owner of the land with the right to sub-let or transfer it, provided he paid the revenue. Its beginnings lie in the Baramahal tract (present-day Tamil Nadu) in the 1790s under Captain Alexander Read, who was soon assisted by Thomas Munro. Munro, as Governor of Madras (1820-27), generalised the system across the Madras Presidency from 1820. It was later extended to Bombay (Elphinstone, with the Pringle survey), and the revenue was periodically revised, typically every 20-30 years, which made it burdensome. The third system, the Mahalwari System (1822, Holt Mackenzie; refined by Regulation of 1833 and Robert Merttins Bird), was for North-Western Provinces, with the village (mahal) as the unit. Elimination logic: Cornwallis is linked with the Permanent Settlement, so statement 1 is out; this removes (a), (b) and (d), leaving (c).
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong: Cornwallis is tied to the Permanent Settlement, and this option also leaves out Read and Munro, who are the actual Ryotwari figures.
(b) 1 and 3 only is wrong: it wrongly includes Cornwallis and omits Alexander Read, who pioneered the system.
(c) 2 and 3 only is correct: Alexander Read and Thomas Munro were both associated with introducing the Ryotwari Settlement.
(d) 1, 2 and 3 is wrong: it includes Cornwallis, who was associated with the Permanent Settlement of Bengal.
keyfact: Ryotwari = Alexander Read (Baramahal) + Thomas Munro (Madras, 1820); Cornwallis = Permanent Settlement 1793.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement (Zamindari system) in 1793 in Bengal, not the Ryotwari system.
2 — Correct: Alexander Read first experimented with the ryotwari arrangement in the Baramahal region in the 1790s.
3 — Correct: Thomas Munro extended and implemented the Ryotwari system in the Madras Presidency, especially from 1820 as Governor.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 2 and 3 only. The Ryotwari Settlement was pioneered by Alexander Read in the Baramahal region and then extended across Madras Presidency by Thomas Munro, whereas Lord Cornwallis is associated with the Permanent Settlement (Zamindari system) of 1793 in Bengal.

question:
In the context of solving pollution problems, 18, what is/are the advantage/advantages of bioremediation technique ?
1. It is a technique for cleaning up pollution by enhancing the same biodegradation process that occurs in nature.
2. Any contaminant with heavy metals such as cadmium and lead can be readily and completely treated by bioremediation using microorganisms. 83. Genetic engineering can be used to create microorganisms specifically designed for 19. bioremediation. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Environment
detail: Bioremediation uses living organisms, mainly bacteria and fungi (and plants in phytoremediation), to degrade or transform contaminants into less toxic forms. It works by enhancing natural biodegradation, for example by adding nutrients (biostimulation) or adding specialised microbes (bioaugmentation). It is used for oil spills, petroleum hydrocarbons, pesticides and solvents. Genetic engineering has produced strains for this purpose; the classic example is the Ananda Chakrabarty 'oil-eating' Pseudomonas, the subject of the 1980 US Supreme Court case Diamond v. Chakrabarty. The key limitation is that heavy metals such as cadmium, lead and mercury are elements and cannot be broken down. Microbes can only change their oxidation state, mobilise them or immobilise them (biosorption, bioaccumulation), so treatment is neither ready nor complete. Elimination logic: statement 2 uses absolute words ('any', 'readily', 'completely'), which is a red flag, so it is wrong. This removes options (b) and (d). Statement 1 is the textbook definition, so it is correct, leaving (c) once statement 3 is confirmed as correct. Option (a) fails because it ignores statement 3.
explanations: (a) is wrong: statement 1 is correct, but statement 3 is also correct, so '1 only' is incomplete.
(b) is wrong: it includes statement 2, which is false because heavy metals cannot be completely degraded by microbes.
(c) is right: statements 1 and 3 are correct, and statement 2 is false.
(d) is wrong: it includes statement 2, which wrongly claims that any heavy-metal contaminant can be readily and completely treated.
keyfact: Bioremediation enhances natural biodegradation and can use engineered microbes, but it cannot fully destroy heavy metals like cadmium and lead.
statements: 1 — Correct: Bioremediation enhances the same natural biodegradation processes using microbes, nutrients and oxygen.
2 — Incorrect: Heavy metals like cadmium and lead are non-degradable, so microbes cannot readily or completely treat them; the words 'any' and 'completely' make the claim false.
3 — Correct: Genetically engineered microorganisms, such as Chakrabarty's Pseudomonas strain, can be designed for specific bioremediation tasks.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. Bioremediation speeds up natural biodegradation, and genetically engineered microbes can be designed for it, but heavy metals such as cadmium and lead cannot be readily or completely removed by microbes.

question: The Trade Disputes Act of 1929 provided for
options: the participation of workers in the management of industries. :
arbitrary powers to the management to quell industrial disputes
an intervention by the British Court in the event of a trade dispute. 20
a system of tribunals and a ban on strikes
subject: Economy
detail: The Trade Disputes Act, 1929 was enacted by the colonial government, alongside the Public Safety Bill, in the backdrop of rising labour militancy and communist influence in the late 1920s (the Bombay textile strikes of 1928, the Girni Kamgar Union, and the Meerut Conspiracy Case of 1929). The Act made provision for Courts of Inquiry and Boards of Conciliation for investigating and settling disputes, which is the tribunal-like machinery referred to in the option. Its most controversial part was the restriction on strikes: strikes in public utility services (railways, posts, water, electricity and so on) required a month's notice, and any strike which went beyond the trade dispute in question or aimed to coerce the government, including general and sympathetic strikes, was declared illegal. It was a precursor of later laws such as the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Elimination: workers' participation in management (a) was a post-Independence idea, seen in the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 and later works committees and the 1970s-80s schemes. Option (b) is too broad, since the Act did not give management arbitrary power. Option (c) is wrong because the Act set up Indian-administered statutory conciliation and inquiry bodies, not intervention by a British court.
explanations: Incorrect: Workers' participation in management was not a feature of the 1929 Act; it came in later labour policy, such as works committees under the Industrial Disputes Act 1947.

Incorrect: The Act did not give management arbitrary powers; it created a statutory process of inquiry and conciliation and restricted strikes, which were the state's instruments rather than the employers'.
Incorrect: The Act set up Courts of Inquiry and Boards of Conciliation within India; it did not provide for intervention by a British court.
Correct: The Act provided for Courts of Inquiry and Boards of Conciliation and banned strikes in public utility services without notice, along with sympathetic and general strikes.
keyfact: Trade Disputes Act 1929: Courts of Inquiry and Conciliation Boards plus a ban on strikes in public utilities without notice and on general or sympathetic strikes.
summary: The correct answer is (d). The Trade Disputes Act, 1929 provided for Courts of Inquiry and Boards of Conciliation to settle industrial disputes, and it made strikes illegal in public utility services unless advance notice was given, and also outlawed sympathetic and general strikes.

question: Local self-government can be best explained as an exercise in
subject: Polity
detail: Democratic decentralisation means devolution of political, administrative and financial authority to elected bodies closest to the people, who are accountable to the local electorate. In India, the Balwantrai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended the three-tier Panchayati Raj, and the Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) suggested a two-tier structure. The 73rd Amendment (1992, in force 24 April 1993) added Part IX and Articles 243 to 243-O and the Eleventh Schedule with 29 subjects. The 74th Amendment added Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule with 18 subjects for municipalities. Key features include regular elections every five years, State Election Commissions, State Finance Commissions, reservation for SCs, STs and women (at least one-third), and Gram Sabha. Article 40 (DPSP) directs the State to organise village panchayats. Elimination: federalism concerns constitutional division of powers between Union and States, and local bodies are not a separate constitutionally sovereign tier in that sense. Administrative delegation merely assigns tasks within a hierarchy, without autonomy or elected accountability. Direct democracy means citizens decide directly, as in referendums, whereas local bodies work through elected representatives, with Gram Sabha being only a partial exception.
explanations: Incorrect: Federalism is the division of powers between the Union and the States; local governments are created and empowered by constitutional amendment and State legislation, and are not a federal partner in the classical sense.
Correct: Local self-government devolves powers, functions and funds to elected local bodies, which is the essence of democratic decentralisation.

Incorrect: Administrative delegation transfers duties to subordinate officials who remain accountable to superiors, with no autonomy or elected representation; local self-government is more than that.
Incorrect: Direct democracy involves citizens deciding issues directly (referendum, initiative, recall); local bodies operate through elected representatives, so this does not best describe them.
keyfact: 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) gave constitutional status to Panchayats and Municipalities, embodying democratic decentralisation.
summary: The answer is (b) Democratic decentralisation. Local self-government, institutionalised through the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments, transfers power, functions and finances to elected local bodies, so that people govern themselves at the grassroots.

question: Consider the following statements : With reference to the Constitution of India, the Directive Principles of State Policy constitute limitations upon AF legislative function. 2. executive function. Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: DPSPs are in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Constitution, borrowed from the Irish Constitution. Article 37 says they are not enforceable by any court, though they are fundamental in the governance of the country, and it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws. Because they are non-justiciable, a law cannot be struck down merely for violating a DPSP, and the executive cannot be restrained by a court for ignoring one. This is the contrast with Fundamental Rights (Part III), which are justiciable and operate as real limitations on legislative and executive action under Article 13. The UPSC's framing of 'limitations' is the trap: DPSPs are positive directions and ideals that guide policy, not restrictions that bar action. Key case law: in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) the Supreme Court held that Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs. Later, Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980) stressed harmony and balance between the two parts. Article 31C gives limited protection to laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c). Elimination logic: once you know DPSPs are non-justiciable and merely directive, both statements fail, and (a), (b) and (c) fall away.
explanations: (a) is wrong because DPSPs are not enforceable limitations on legislative power; only Fundamental Rights and constitutional provisions such as federal distribution of powers limit it.
(b) is wrong because DPSPs do not constitute enforceable limits on executive functions either; they are only moral and political guidelines.
(c) is wrong because neither statement holds. Both treat DPSPs as binding limitations, contrary to Article 37.
(d) is correct because DPSPs are non-justiciable directives, so they limit neither legislative nor executive functions in a legally enforceable way.
keyfact: Article 37: DPSPs are non-justiciable, so they guide but do not limit the legislature or the executive, unlike Fundamental Rights.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: DPSPs are non-justiciable (Article 37). They guide the legislature but do not bind it or limit its power, and courts cannot invalidate a law solely for violating them.
2 — Incorrect: The executive is likewise not legally restrained by DPSPs. They are directions for policy-making, not enforceable limits on executive action.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs) are non-justiciable guidelines for the State. They do not impose enforceable limitations on either legislative or executive functions.

ocr: The term ‘Digital Single Market Strategy’ seen in the news refers to (a) ASEAN (b) BRICS (c) EU (d) G20 At one of the places in India, if you stand on the seashore and watch the sea, you will find that the sea water recedes from the shore line a few kilometres and comes back to the shore, twice a day, and you can actually walk on the sea floor when the water recedes. This unique phenomenon is seen at (a) Bhavnagar (b) Bheemunipatnam (c) Chandipur (d) Nagapattinam
subject: Geography
detail: The Digital Single Market Strategy was adopted by the European Commission in May 2015 under President Jean-Claude Juncker. It aims to let individuals and businesses access and carry out online activity fairly and easily across the 28 member states, then including the UK, without barriers such as geo-blocking and differing national rules. It rests on three pillars: (1) better access to digital goods and services for consumers and businesses, including cross-border e-commerce rules, parcel delivery and ending unjustified geo-blocking; (2) the right conditions for digital networks and services, including telecom reform, data protection and platform regulation; and (3) maximising the growth potential of the digital economy, including the free flow of data, cloud computing, standards and e-skills. It builds on the EU single market of free movement of goods, services, capital and people. Later outcomes include the end of mobile roaming charges in June 2017, portability of online content and the GDPR, which took effect in May 2018. Elimination logic: 'Single Market' is characteristic EU terminology. ASEAN has an Economic Community, BRICS and G20 are not single-market blocs, and none of them has a Commission-driven digital strategy. Note that the next question on the page (the sea receding twice a day) is also answered (c), Chandipur in Odisha.
explanations: Incorrect: ASEAN has the ASEAN Economic Community and a Master Plan on Connectivity, but not a 'Digital Single Market Strategy'.
Incorrect: BRICS is a grouping of emerging economies (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa) with no single-market framework or digital strategy of this kind.
Correct: the European Union launched the Digital Single Market Strategy in 2015 to unify digital regulation and commerce across member states.
Incorrect: the G20 is a forum for economic policy coordination among major economies, not an integrated market with its own digital single-market strategy.
keyfact: Digital Single Market Strategy = European Union (European Commission, May 2015); the follow-on question's answer is Chandipur, Odisha, where the sea recedes several km twice a day.
summary: The answer is (c) EU. The Digital Single Market (DSM) Strategy was launched by the European Commission in May 2015 to remove digital barriers between EU member states and create a single digital market.

question:
With reference to the ‘Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 (PBPT Act)’, consider the following statements :
1. A property transaction is not treated as a benami transaction if the owner of the property is not aware of the transaction.
2. Properties held benami are liable for confiscation by the Government.
3. The Act provides for three authorities for investigations but does not provide for any appellate mechanism. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 was substantially amended by the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016, in force from 1 November 2016. It bans benami transactions, where property is held by one person for the benefit of another who paid the consideration. The Act allows the property to be confiscated by the Central Government without compensation. Section 2(9) defines a benami transaction and excludes only specific cases: property held by a coparcener in a Hindu undivided family, by a person in a fiduciary capacity such as a trustee or agent, by an individual in the name of a spouse or child bought from known income, and by siblings in joint ownership. An owner's lack of awareness is not an exclusion. The definition actually covers property held in the name of a fictitious person, or by someone who denies or is unaware of the ownership. The enforcement machinery has Initiating Officers, Approving Authorities and Administrators, an Adjudicating Authority, and an Appellate Tribunal, with a further appeal to the High Court. Elimination: statement 3 is false, so (c) and (d) fall away. Statement 1 is also false, so (a) falls away. That leaves (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because the owner's unawareness does not take a transaction out of the benami definition, and statement 2 is correct but is left out.
(b) is correct on the law: only statement 2 holds, since benami properties can be confiscated. This is also what I recall as the published UPSC key.

(c) is wrong: it requires statements 1 and 3 to be correct, but both are incorrect, and statement 3 ignores the Adjudicating Authority and Appellate Tribunal. It matches the supplied key but not the Act.
(d) is wrong: statement 2 is correct, but statement 3 is false because the Act has an appellate mechanism.
keyfact: The PBPT Act (amended 2016) allows confiscation of benami property and provides an Adjudicating Authority and Appellate Tribunal, so the correct option is (b) 2 only; the supplied key (c) conflicts with the Act.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Lack of awareness by the owner is not an exclusion under Section 2(9). Property held by someone who is unaware or denies knowledge of ownership is within the benami definition.
2 — Correct: Under Section 27, benami property is liable to confiscation by the Central Government, and the 2016 amendment strengthened this.
3 — Incorrect: The Act provides an Adjudicating Authority and an Appellate Tribunal, with a further appeal to the High Court, so it does have an appellate mechanism.
summary: The key supplied says (c), but on the law as it stands only statement 2 is correct, which is option (b). I recall UPSC's published key also gave (b). Statement 3 is plainly wrong, because the Act sets up an Adjudicating Authority and an Appellate Tribunal, so (c) cannot be right.

ocr: With reference to the ‘Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 (PBPT Act)’, consider the following statements : 1. A property transaction is not treated as a benami transaction if the owner of the property is not aware of the transaction. 2. Properties held benami are liable for confiscation by the Government. 3. The Act provides for three authorities for investigations but does not provide for any appellate mechanism. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) lonly (b) 2only (c) land 3 only (d) 2and 3 only
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The PBPT Act, 1988 prohibits benami transactions, where property is held by one person (the benamidar) while consideration is paid by another (the beneficial owner). The 2016 Amendment Act, in force from 1 November 2016, strengthened it substantially. Benami property is liable to confiscation by the Central Government without compensation (Section 27). Entering into a benami transaction is punishable with imprisonment of 1 to 7 years and a fine (Section 53). The Act sets up adjudicating and investigative machinery: Initiating Officer, Approving Authority and Administrator, who are the authorities for investigation and attachment, and the Adjudicating Authority, which examines attachments. Appeals against the Adjudicating Authority's orders lie to the Appellate Tribunal, and further to the High Court. Hence a claim that the Act has no appellate mechanism is wrong. Statement 1 is also wrong, because the definition of a benami transaction turns on the property being held by one person for consideration provided by another. Exceptions exist, such as property held by a person in a fiduciary capacity, or in the name of a spouse or child, where consideration comes from known income sources. The owner's lack of awareness is not an exemption. Elimination: statement 2 is certainly correct, and statement 3 fails because an appellate tribunal exists, which leaves only option (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect: an owner's lack of awareness does not stop a transaction from being treated as benami.
(b) is right because only statement 2 is correct: benami property can be confiscated by the Government, while statements 1 and 3 are wrong.
(c) is wrong because it includes statements 1 and 3, both of which are incorrect, and it leaves out the correct statement 2.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 3, which wrongly denies an appellate mechanism, even though statement 2 is correct.
keyfact: PBPT Act 1988 (amended 2016, effective 1 Nov 2016): benami property is liable to confiscation, with an Adjudicating Authority and an Appellate Tribunal for appeals.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The owner's unawareness does not take a transaction outside the Act. The test is whether property is held by one person for consideration paid by another, and the Act contains no exemption for an unaware owner.
2 — Correct: Under Section 27, benami property is liable to confiscation by the Central Government, and the 2016 amendment made this a central feature of the law.

3 — Incorrect: The Act provides an appellate mechanism, namely the Adjudicating Authority and then the Appellate Tribunal, with a further appeal to the High Court. It is therefore wrong to say there is no appellate mechanism.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 2 only. Under the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 (as amended in 2016, effective 1 November 2016), benami property is liable to confiscation by the Government, but a transaction is not saved merely because the real owner is unaware, and the Act does provide an appellate mechanism.

question:
Due to some reasons, if there is a huge fall in 28. the population of species of butterflies, what could be its likely consequence/consequences ? 1, Pollination of some plants could be adversely affected. 2 There could be a drastic increase in the fungal infections of some cultivated plants.
3. It could lead to a fall in the population of some species of wasps, spiders and birds. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Environment
detail: This question tests ecological interdependence and food-web logic. Butterflies are pollinators, so their decline can reduce pollination, seed set and reproduction in plants that depend on them (statement 1). Butterflies and their caterpillars are also a food source in the food web. Birds, spiders and many wasps prey on them, and parasitoid wasps lay eggs in or on caterpillars. A large fall in butterfly numbers would therefore reduce food and hosts for these consumers, lowering some of their populations (statement 3). Statement 2 is the odd one out. Fungal infections of crops are caused by fungal pathogens whose spread depends on humidity, temperature, spores and plant susceptibility, not on butterfly numbers. Butterflies are not recognised as natural controllers of fungi, so a 'drastic increase' is an unsupported leap. In UPSC elimination logic, extreme words such as 'drastic' signal a likely wrong statement. Since 1 and 3 are sound and 2 is not, only (c) fits. Options (a), (b) and (d) each wrongly drop statement 3 or wrongly include statement 2. Remember that pollinators sit at both ends of food-web effects: they affect plants and also feed predators.
explanations: (a) is wrong: it omits statement 3, which is valid because predators and parasitoids depend on butterflies and their larvae.
(b) is wrong: it includes statement 2, which is unsupported, and leaves out statement 1, which is correct.
(c) is right: statements 1 (pollination) and 3 (food-web effects on wasps, spiders, birds) hold, while statement 2 does not.
(d) is wrong: it includes statement 2, a drastic fungal increase, which has no ecological basis from butterfly decline.
keyfact: Butterflies are both pollinators and prey/hosts, so their decline hits plants and predators, but it does not cause crop fungal outbreaks.
statements: 1 — Correct: Butterflies are pollinators, so a huge decline would adversely affect the pollination of some plants.
2 — Incorrect: There is no established link between butterfly decline and a drastic rise in fungal infections of crops; fungal disease depends on pathogens and environmental conditions.
3 — Correct: Butterflies and caterpillars are prey or hosts for wasps (including parasitoids), spiders and birds, so their populations could fall.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. A sharp decline in butterflies would affect plant pollination and the predators that feed on them or their larvae, but there is no established link between butterfly decline and a drastic rise in fungal infections of crops.

ocr: It is possible to produce algae based biofuels, but what is/are the likely limitation(s) of developing countries in promoting this industry ? 1. Production of algae based biofuels is possible in seas only and not on continents. 2 Setting: up and engineering the algae based biofuel production requires high level of expertise/technology until the 25. construction is completed. 3. Economically viable production necessitates the setting up of large scale facilities which may raise ecological and social concerns. Seiect the correct answer using the code given below : (a) land 2 only (b) 2and 3 only
subject: Economy
detail: Algae-based biofuels (third-generation biofuels) are made from micro- and macro-algae, which are rich in lipids that can be converted into biodiesel, bioethanol or biogas. Algae grow fast, need little land, and do not compete with food crops. They can be cultivated in open raceway ponds, closed photobioreactors, wastewater, brackish or saline water, and on marginal or non-arable land, so cultivation is not limited to the sea. Constraints are mainly techno-economic. Photobioreactor design, strain selection, harvesting, dewatering and lipid extraction need advanced engineering and capital, which many developing countries lack.
