statements: 1 — Incorrect: Viruses are extremely abundant in ocean waters, mostly phages infecting marine microbes, and they play a key role in nutrient cycling.
2 — Incorrect: Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria.
3 — Incorrect: Many viruses, such as retroviruses, HPV and influenza, alter host transcriptional activity to favour their own replication.
summary: The answer is (d) None. All three statements are false: viruses are abundant in ocean waters, bacteriophages infect bacteria, and many viruses reprogram host-cell transcription.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I : Activated carbon is a good and an attractive tool to remove pollutants from effluent streams and to remediate contaminants from various industries.
Statement II : Activated carbon exhibits a large surface area and a strong potential for adsorbing heavy metals. Statement III : Activated carbon can be easily synthesized from environmental wastes with high carbon content. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement II and Statement III are correct and both of them explain Statement I
Both Statement II and Statement Il are correct but only one of them explains Statement I
Only one of the Statements II and Ill is correct and that explains Statement I
Neither Statement II nor Statement Ill is correct [ P.T.O
subject: Environment
detail: Activated carbon is a highly porous form of carbon, produced by carbonising and then activating (physically with steam or CO2, or chemically with agents such as H3PO4 or KOH) carbon-rich precursors. The porous structure gives a surface area often exceeding 500 to 1500 m2 per gram, which provides abundant sites for adsorption. Adsorption means pollutants adhere to the surface, unlike absorption. It removes heavy metals (lead, cadmium, chromium, mercury, arsenic), dyes, phenols, pesticides, and organic and volatile compounds from industrial effluents, drinking water and air. It is available as granular (GAC) and powdered (PAC) forms. Feedstocks include agricultural residues such as coconut shells, rice husk, sugarcane bagasse and nut shells, as well as wood, coal and sewage sludge. Using such wastes makes it cheap and supports a circular economy, since waste is converted into a pollution-control material. In this type of question, check each statement for factual accuracy first, then ask whether the statements give the reasons for Statement I. Statement II gives the technical effectiveness and Statement III gives the economic and practical availability. Both are valid reasons for calling it a good and attractive tool, so options (b), (c) and (d) are eliminated.
explanations: (a) Correct: both Statements II and III are true, and together they explain Statement I, since effectiveness (II) and low-cost availability (III) make it attractive.
(b) Wrong: it says only one of the two statements explains Statement I, but both do, covering technical performance and economic feasibility.
(c) Wrong: both statements are correct, so saying only one is correct is false.
(d) Wrong: both statements are factually correct, so denying them is false.
keyfact: Activated carbon: porous, huge surface area, adsorbs heavy metals and organics, and is cheaply made from carbon-rich wastes.
statements: 1 — Correct: Activated carbon is widely used to treat effluents and remediate contaminants from industries.
2 — Correct: Its large surface area and porosity give strong adsorption of heavy metals, which explains its effectiveness.
3 — Correct: It can be easily and cheaply made from carbon-rich wastes such as coconut shells, husks and bagasse, which explains why it is attractive.
summary: The answer is (a). Activated carbon has a very large surface area and a strong capacity to adsorb heavy metals (Statement II), and it can be made cheaply from carbon-rich wastes (Statement III). Together these explain why it is a good and attractive tool for removing pollutants (Statement I).

question:
With reference to the Indian polity, consider the following statements :
I. An Ordinance can amend any Central Act. Il. An Ordinance can abridge a Fundamental Right. Ill. An Ordinance can come into effect from a back date. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate Ordinances when Parliament is not in session (either House not in session, in fact) and he is satisfied that circumstances require immediate action. Article 123(2) says an Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, but only in respect of matters on which Parliament can legislate. It must be laid before Parliament and ceases to operate six weeks after Parliament reassembles, or earlier if both Houses disapprove it. Because it has the force of an Act, it can amend or repeal any Central Act, and it can be given retrospective effect, including in tax matters. Article 13(3)(a) defines 'law' to include an Ordinance, and Article 13(2) forbids the State from making any law that takes away or abridges Fundamental Rights. So an Ordinance cannot abridge a Fundamental Right, which makes statement II wrong. Elimination logic: II is false, so options (a), (b) and (d) all fall away, leaving (c). Also remember that an Ordinance cannot amend the Constitution. The Court in D.C. Wadhwa (1987) condemned the repeated re-promulgation of Ordinances as a fraud on the Constitution, and Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) held that the legislative necessity must be examined.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes II, which is incorrect, and leaves out III, which is correct.
(b) is wrong because it includes II, which is incorrect, and leaves out I, which is correct.
(c) is correct because I and III are right and II is wrong; an Ordinance is bound by Art. 13(2).
(d) is wrong because it includes statement II, but an Ordinance cannot abridge a Fundamental Right.
keyfact: An Ordinance (Art. 123) equals an Act in force, so it can amend Central Acts and operate retrospectively, but it is 'law' under Art. 13 and cannot abridge Fundamental Rights or amend the Constitution.
statements: I — Correct: An Ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament (Art. 123(2)), so it can amend or repeal any Central Act, subject to the limits on Parliament's own power.
II — Incorrect: 'Law' in Art. 13(3)(a) includes an Ordinance, and Art. 13(2) bars any law that takes away or abridges Fundamental Rights.
III — Correct: Like an Act, an Ordinance can have retrospective effect, since Parliament's legislative power includes making laws operate from a back date.
summary: The answer is (c): statements I and III are correct, and statement II is incorrect. An Ordinance under Article 123 has the same force and limits as an Act of Parliament, so it can amend Central Acts and can be made retrospective, but it cannot abridge Fundamental Rights because Article 13(2) bars any 'law' from doing so.

question:
Consider the following pairs : State Description
I. Arunachal : The capital is named after Pradesh a fort, and the State has two National Parks Il. Nagaland : The State came into existence on the basis of a Constitutional Amendment Act Il. Tripura : Initially a Part ‘C’ State, it became a centrally administered territory with the reorganization of States in 1956 and later attained the status of a full-fledged State How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
subject: Polity
detail: Pair I: Itanagar, the capital of Arunachal Pradesh, takes its name from the Ita Fort (brick fort, 14th-15th century). The State has two National Parks, Namdapha (Changlang district) and Mouling (Upper Siang district), so the description holds. Arunachal, formerly NEFA, became a Union Territory in 1972 and a State in 1987 via the 55th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1986. Pair II: Nagaland was formed as the 16th State by the State of Nagaland Act, 1962, enacted under the 13th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962, which inserted Article 371A, giving special protection to Naga customary law, religious and social practices, and land ownership. It became a State on 1 December 1963. Pair III: Under the 1950 Constitution Tripura was a Part C State. The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 and the 7th Amendment made it a Union Territory, and the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971 made it a full State on 21 January 1972, together with Manipur and Meghalaya. Since all three descriptions are factually accurate, options (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it implies only one pair is correct, but all three pairs are accurate.
(b) Wrong: it implies one pair is incorrect, but none is.
(c) Right: all three pairs are correctly matched, in line with the official answer.
(d) Wrong: it implies no pair is correct, which contradicts the facts for all three states.
keyfact: Nagaland: 13th Amendment 1962 (Art. 371A); Tripura: Part C, then UT 1956, then State 1972; Itanagar is named after Ita Fort.
statements: 1 — Correct: Itanagar is named after Ita Fort, and Arunachal Pradesh has two National Parks, Namdapha and Mouling.
2 — Correct: Nagaland was created by the 13th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962 (Article 371A) and the State of Nagaland Act, 1962, and became a State in 1963.
3 — Correct: Tripura was a Part C State, became a Union Territory in 1956, and attained full statehood in 1972.
summary: The answer is (c): all three pairs are correctly matched. Itanagar is named after Ita Fort, Nagaland was created through the 13th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962, and Tripura moved from Part C State to Union Territory (1956) to full statehood (1972).

question:
With reference to India, consider the following :
I. The Inter-State Council
II. The National Security Council Ill. Zonal Councils How many of the above’ were established as per the provisions of the Constitution of India?
subject: Polity
detail: The question tests the difference between constitutional bodies, statutory bodies and executive (non-statutory) bodies. Article 263 empowers the President to establish an Inter-State Council if it appears that the public interest would be served by one. It would investigate and discuss subjects of common interest between States, or between the Union and States, and make recommendations. The Council was actually set up in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation. Its constitutional source is Article 263, so it counts as established as per the Constitution's provisions. Zonal Councils (five originally: Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, Southern; the North-Eastern Council was created separately by the North Eastern Council Act, 1971) were set up under Part III of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. They are statutory, not constitutional. The National Security Council was constituted in 1998 by an executive resolution of the Government of India, with the Prime Minister as chair. It has no constitutional or statutory backing. Elimination: since Zonal Councils and the NSC are not constitutional, options (b) and (c) fail. Since the Inter-State Council is constitutional under Article 263, option (d) fails. This leaves (a).
explanations: Correct. Only the Inter-State Council (Article 263) is established under the Constitution, so exactly one of the three qualifies.
Wrong. Two cannot qualify, because Zonal Councils (statutory, 1956 Act) and the NSC (executive, 1998) lack a constitutional basis.
Wrong. All three would require the NSC and Zonal Councils to be constitutional, and they are not.
Wrong. The Inter-State Council is constitutional under Article 263, so at least one qualifies.
keyfact: Inter-State Council = Article 263 (constitutional); Zonal Councils = States Reorganisation Act 1956 (statutory); NSC = 1998 executive decision (non-statutory).
statements: 1 — Correct: The Inter-State Council is provided for under Article 263 of the Constitution, and the President may establish it. It was set up in 1990.
2 — Incorrect: The National Security Council was created in 1998 by an executive decision. It has no constitutional or statutory basis.
3 — Incorrect: Zonal Councils are statutory bodies set up by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, not by the Constitution.
summary: The answer is (a) Only one. Of the three bodies, only the Inter-State Council has a basis in the Constitution (Article 263). The National Security Council was set up by an executive decision in 1998, and Zonal Councils were created by a statute, the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

question:
Consider the following statements :
I. The Constitution of India explicitly mentions that in certain spheres the Governor of a State acts in his/her own discretion. Il. The President of India can, of his/her own, reserve a bill passed by a State Legislature for his/her consideration without it being forwarded by the Governor of the State concerned. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 163(1) says the Governor acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers 'except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion'. Express discretion appears in the Sixth Schedule (Para 9(2): the Governor of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram determines the share of royalty between the District Council and the State), and under Article 371-A, 371-H and similar special provisions (e.g., Nagaland law and order, Sikkim). Article 163(2) makes the Governor's decision on whether a matter falls within his discretion final. Under Article 200, the Governor may assent, withhold assent, return a non-money bill for reconsideration, or reserve a bill for the President. Article 201 then lets the President act only on a bill reserved by the Governor: assent, withhold assent, or direct its return. The Constitution gives the President no power to call up or reserve a State bill suo motu, unlike the Union's power to disallow State laws in other contexts. Hence Statement I is correct and II is incorrect, which eliminates (b), (c) and (d).
explanations: Correct: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, so 'I only' is right.
Wrong: Statement II is false because the President cannot reserve a State bill without the Governor forwarding it, and Statement I is true.
Wrong: Statement II is not correct, so both cannot be right.
Wrong: Statement I is correct, since the Constitution expressly mentions Governor's discretion.
keyfact: Governor's discretion is explicit in Art. 163(1) and the Sixth Schedule, but only the Governor can reserve a State bill for the President (Art. 200-201).
statements: 1 — Correct: Article 163(1) and provisions such as Sixth Schedule Para 9(2) and Articles 371-A and 371-H expressly provide for Governor's discretion.
2 — Incorrect: Under Articles 200-201, a bill reaches the President only when the Governor reserves it; the President has no power to reserve a State bill on his/her own.
summary: The answer is (a): only Statement I is correct. The Constitution explicitly provides for the Governor's discretion in certain spheres (e.g., Article 163(1) and the Sixth Schedule), but the President cannot reserve a State bill on his/her own, because reservation under Article 200 is initiated only by the Governor.

question: Consider the following pairs : Stated under Provision in the Constitution of India The Directive Separation of Judiciary Principles from the Executive in of the State the public services of Policy the State The FundaValuing and preserving Il. mental Duties of the rich heritage of our composite culture : The FundaProhibition of employIll. mental Rights ment of children below the age of 14 years in factories above pairs are How many of the correctly matched?
subject: Polity
detail: Each pair matches a provision to the part of the Constitution where it appears. Article 50 in Part IV (Directive Principles) directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State. Article 51A(f) in Part IVA (Fundamental Duties, added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation) makes it a duty of every citizen to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture. Article 24 in Part III (Fundamental Rights, under the Right against Exploitation, Articles 23-24) prohibits employing children below 14 years in factories, mines or other hazardous employment. Note that Article 21A (free and compulsory education for ages 6-14, 86th Amendment 2002) and Article 45 (early childhood care) are separate provisions. The elimination logic is to verify each pair against its article number. Since all three are verifiable, 'None', 'Only one' and 'Only two' are all ruled out, leaving (d). If the official key really says (c), that would contradict the text above, so recheck the OCR of the question and the key.
explanations: (a) Only two: Wrong on the constitutional text, because no pair is mismatched, so the count cannot be two.
(b) Only one: Wrong, because all three pairs are correct, not just one.
(c) None: This is the key supplied with the question, but it conflicts with Articles 50, 51A(f) and 24, which make every pair correct. Verify against the official answer key.
(d) All the three: Correct on the constitutional text, since Article 50 (DPSP), Article 51A(f) (Duties) and Article 24 (Fundamental Rights) match the three pairs.
keyfact: Art. 50 = separation of judiciary from executive (DPSP); Art. 51A(f) = composite culture (Duty); Art. 24 = no child labour under 14 in factories/mines (FR).
statements: I — Correct: Article 50 (DPSP) provides for separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
II — Correct: Article 51A(f) (Fundamental Duties) requires citizens to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture.
III — Correct: Article 24 (Fundamental Right against Exploitation) prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines or hazardous work.
summary: On the constitutional text, all three pairs are correctly matched, which is option (d). The key supplied with this question says (c), but that does not fit Articles 50, 51A(f) and 24, so please check it against the official UPSC answer key before filing this note.

question: Consider the following statements : With reference to the Constitution of India, if an area in a State is declared as Scheduled Area under the Fifth Schedule I. the State Government loses its executive power in such areas and a local body assumes total administration Il. the Union Government can take over the total administration of such areas under certain circumstances on the recommendations of the Governor Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 244(1) applies the Fifth Schedule to the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in States other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, which are covered by the Sixth Schedule. The President declares Scheduled Areas under Para 6 of the Fifth Schedule, after consulting the Governor of the State concerned. The State's executive power continues in these areas. Para 3 requires the Governor to report annually, or whenever required by the President, on the administration of Scheduled Areas, and the Union's executive power extends to giving directions to the State on their administration. Para 4 provides for a Tribes Advisory Council. The Governor may direct that a particular Act of Parliament or the State Legislature does not apply to a Scheduled Area, or applies with modifications (Para 5). The Governor may also make regulations for peace and good government, for example on land transfer by tribals and the regulation of moneylending (Para 5(2)). No local body assumes total administration; autonomous district and regional councils belong to the Sixth Schedule, and PESA 1996 empowers gram sabhas in Fifth Schedule areas. No provision allows the Union to take over administration on the Governor's recommendation. Article 356 is a separate matter and is invoked on the Governor's report of constitutional breakdown, not under the Fifth Schedule. Both statements are therefore wrong.
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement I is incorrect: the State keeps its executive power, and no local body assumes total administration of a Fifth Schedule area.
(b) is wrong because Statement II is incorrect: the Union can only give directions to the State, and cannot take over total administration under the Fifth Schedule.
(c) is wrong because neither statement is correct, so they cannot both be right.
(d) is correct because both statements misdescribe the Fifth Schedule: the State's executive power continues, and the Union's role is limited to giving directions.
keyfact: In Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas the State executive continues to function under the Governor's special powers (Paras 3-5) and Union directions; autonomous councils belong to the Sixth Schedule.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The State government retains executive power in Scheduled Areas. The Governor has special responsibilities and regulation-making powers, and autonomous councils with administrative powers are a Sixth Schedule feature, not a Fifth Schedule one.

2 — Incorrect: The Fifth Schedule gives the Union only the power to give directions to the State on administering Scheduled Areas. It has no provision for taking over total administration on the Governor's recommendation.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. Declaring an area a Scheduled Area under the Fifth Schedule does not strip the State of its executive power, and the Union has no provision to take over total administration on the Governor's recommendation.

question:
With reference to India, consider the following pairs : Organization Union Ministry
I. The National : Ministry of Automotive Board Commerce and Industry II: The Coir Board : Ministry of Heavy Industries Ill. The National : Ministry of Micro, Centre for Trade Small and Medium Information Enterprises How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
subject: Economy
detail: This question tests whether you know which ministry administers which body, and here the ministries in the question were deliberately swapped around. The National Automotive Board (NAB) was set up to support the automotive sector, including testing and homologation, and it works under the Ministry of Heavy Industries, which handles the automobile industry and schemes such as FAME and PLI for auto. The Coir Board is a statutory body set up under the Coir Industry Act, 1953 to promote the coir industry and exports, and it comes under the Ministry of MSME, which also oversees the KVIC, the National Small Industries Corporation and the Tea, Coffee, Rubber and Spices Boards only in the case of the first-named bodies, while the latter belong to Commerce. The National Centre for Trade Information (NCTI) is run by India Trade Promotion Organisation and the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, and it provides trade information. A good elimination strategy is to check each pair against the ministry's core sector: automobiles map to Heavy Industries, coir to MSME and trade information to Commerce. Since each pair was swapped, none is correct, which makes (d) the answer.
explanations: (a) Wrong: No pair is correctly matched, so 'only one' cannot hold.
(b) Wrong: No pair is correctly matched, so 'only two' cannot hold.
(c) Wrong: All three pairs are mismatched, so they cannot all be correct.
(d) Right: Each pair swaps the ministry, so none of the three is correctly matched.
keyfact: National Automotive Board: Heavy Industries; Coir Board: MSME; National Centre for Trade Information: Commerce and Industry.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The National Automotive Board is under the Ministry of Heavy Industries, not the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
2 — Incorrect: The Coir Board is under the Ministry of MSME, not the Ministry of Heavy Industries.
3 — Incorrect: The National Centre for Trade Information is under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, not the Ministry of MSME.
summary: The answer is (d) None. All three pairs are mismatched: the National Automotive Board is under the Ministry of Heavy Industries, the Coir Board is under the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME), and the National Centre for Trade Information is under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

ocr: Consider the following subjects under the Constitution of India : I. List LUnion List, in the Seventh Schedule Il. Extent of the executive power of a State Ill. Conditions of the Governor’s office For a constitutional amendment with respect to which of the above, ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States is required before presenting the bill to the President of India for assent? (a) 1 and II only (b) 1 and III only (c) 1 and III only (a) 1, Il and Il
subject: Polity
detail: Under Article 368, most constitutional provisions can be amended by a special majority of Parliament: a majority of the total membership of each House, plus two-thirds of members present and voting. Certain 'federal' provisions are entrenched. Under the proviso to Article 368(2), an amendment to them must also be ratified by the legislatures of not less than one-half of the States before the bill is presented to the President for assent. The entrenched matters are: the election of the President (Articles 54 and 55); the extent of the executive power of the Union and the States (Articles 73 and 162); the Supreme Court and High Courts, including Union Territory High Courts (Part V Chapter IV, Part VI Chapter V, Part XI Chapter I); the distribution of legislative powers between Union and States (Part XI, Chapter I); any of the Seventh Schedule Lists; the representation of States in Parliament; and Article 368 itself. Conditions of the Governor's office (Article 158) is not on this list. It can be changed by the special majority alone, so statement III fails. Elimination: statement I and statement II are both entrenched, which removes (b) and (c), and III's exclusion removes (d), leaving (a). Note that the ratification is by simple majority in the State legislatures, with no time limit prescribed.
explanations: Correct: I and II are both listed in the Article 368(2) proviso and need ratification by at least half the States, and III is not.
Wrong: it includes III, which does not need ratification, and leaves out I, which does.
Wrong: it includes III, which does not need ratification, and leaves out II, which does.
Wrong: it includes III, but the conditions of the Governor's office can be amended by Parliament's special majority alone.
keyfact: Article 368(2) proviso: amendments to the Seventh Schedule Lists and to the executive power of the Union and States need ratification by at least half the States; the Governor's office conditions do not.
statements: 1 — Correct: Any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule is covered by the Article 368(2) proviso, so ratification by at least half the States is needed.
2 — Correct: The extent of the executive power of the Union and the States (Articles 73 and 162) is entrenched and needs State ratification.
3 — Incorrect: The conditions of the Governor's office (Article 158) are not in the proviso, so a special majority in Parliament is sufficient.
summary: The answer is (a) I and II only. Article 368(2) requires ratification by the legislatures of at least half the States for amendments touching the Union List in the Seventh Schedule and the extent of the executive power of a State. The conditions of the Governor's office (Article 158) are not in the entrenched list, so a simple Article 368 special majority in Parliament is enough.

question:
With reference to the Indian polity, consider the following statements :
I. The Governor of a State is not answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his/her office. Il. No criminal proceedings shall be instituted or continued against the Governor during his/her term of office. Ill. Members of a State Legislature are not liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said within the House. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 361 deals with the protection of the President and Governors. Clause (1) says the President or a Governor shall not be answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of the office, or for any act done in exercising those powers. Clause (2) says no criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted or continued against the President or a Governor in any court during the term of office. Clause (3) bars arrest or imprisonment of a Governor during the term. Clause (4) allows civil proceedings only after two months' written notice, for personal acts. The Supreme Court in Rameshwar Prasad (2006) held that this immunity does not bar judicial review of the Governor's actions, including a recommendation of President's Rule, and the 2024 West Bengal Governor case also considered the scope of Article 361(2). Article 194(2) gives State legislators immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given in the House or its committees, mirroring Article 105(2) for Parliament. The Governor's immunity concerns his or her person, while the legislators' immunity concerns what they say in the House. Since all three statements match constitutional text, options (a), (b) and (c) fail because each leaves out a correct statement.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it leaves out statement III, and Article 194(2) makes III correct.
(b) is wrong because it leaves out statement I, which Article 361(1) supports.
(c) is wrong because it leaves out statement II, which Article 361(2) supports.
(d) is correct because all three statements match Articles 361(1), 361(2) and 194(2).
keyfact: Article 361 protects the President and Governors (no court answerability, no criminal proceedings in office, civil suits only after 2 months' notice); Article 194(2) protects State legislators' speech in the House.
statements: 1 — Correct: Article 361(1) says the Governor is not answerable to any court for exercising and performing the powers and duties of the office.
2 — Correct: Article 361(2) bars the institution or continuation of criminal proceedings against the Governor during the term of office.
3 — Correct: Article 194(2) says no member of a State Legislature is liable to court proceedings for anything said or any vote given in the Legislature or its committees.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. Article 361 gives the Governor immunity from court answerability and from criminal proceedings during the term of office, and Article 194(2) protects legislators for what they say in the House.

ocr: Consider the following activities : I. Production of crude oil Il. Refining, storage and distribution of petroleum Ill. Marketing and sale of petroleum products IV. Production of natural gas How many of the above activities are regulated by the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board in our country? (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) Only three (ad) All the four [ P.T.O.
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The PNGRB was set up under the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Act, 2006, and began functioning in 2007. Its mandate is to regulate downstream and midstream activities: refining, processing, storage, transportation, distribution, marketing and sale of petroleum, petroleum products and natural gas (excluding production of crude oil and natural gas). It also protects consumer interests, promotes competition, authorises city gas distribution networks and sets pipeline tariffs and access (common carrier/contract carrier). Upstream activities, meaning exploration and production of crude oil and natural gas, are explicitly excluded. They are governed by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, with the Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH) as the technical regulator, under the Oilfields (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, the Petroleum and Natural Gas Rules, 1959, and licensing regimes such as NELP and HELP/OALP. Elimination logic: production items (I and IV) are upstream and so outside PNGRB; items II and III are downstream and so inside PNGRB. That gives exactly two, which is option (b).
explanations: (a) Wrong: Two activities (II and III) are regulated, not just one.
(b) Correct: Only II and III, the downstream and midstream activities, are regulated; production of crude oil and natural gas is excluded.
(c) Wrong: Three would require including either crude oil or natural gas production, both of which the Act excludes.
(d) Wrong: All four would include upstream production, which the PNGRB Act, 2006 does not cover.
keyfact: PNGRB (Act 2006) regulates downstream/midstream petroleum and gas (refining, storage, transport, distribution, marketing) but NOT upstream production of crude oil and natural gas.
statements: I — Incorrect: Production of crude oil is an upstream activity, excluded from PNGRB's remit and handled by the Ministry and DGH.
II — Correct: Refining, storage and distribution of petroleum fall under PNGRB's regulatory mandate.
III — Correct: Marketing and sale of petroleum products are regulated by PNGRB.
IV — Incorrect: Production of natural gas is excluded from PNGRB regulation under the 2006 Act.
summary: The answer is (b) Only two. The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB) regulates refining, processing, storage, transportation, distribution, marketing and sale of petroleum, petroleum products and natural gas, but it does not regulate the production of crude oil and natural gas (upstream).

question:
Suppose the revenue expenditure is 80, 000 crores and the revenue receipts of the Government are 60, 000 crores. The Government budget also shows borrowings of = 10, 000 crores and interest payments of ©€6, 000 crores. Which of the following statements are correct?
I. Revenue deficit is € 20, 000 crores. Il. Fiscal deficit is € 10, 000 crores. Ill. Primary deficit is € 4, 000 crores. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: Three deficit measures are tested here. Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts, so 80,000 - 60,000 = 20,000 crore. It shows the government is not even covering its day-to-day expenses from its current revenue, and is therefore borrowing to meet consumption needs. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings, and it equals the government's net borrowing requirement. The question states borrowings of 10,000 crore, so the fiscal deficit is 10,000 crore. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments = 10,000 - 6,000 = 4,000 crore. It indicates the borrowing needed for current operations, excluding the burden of past debt. A student should remember that the FRBM Act, 2003 sets fiscal deficit targets, and that the Union Budget presents these deficits as part of its fiscal indicators. Elimination logic: once you verify that each of the three statements is arithmetically correct, only the option containing all three (I, II and III) survives. The code in option (d) is garbled by OCR (it reads 1, I and I), but it stands for I, II and III.
explanations: (a) is wrong: it omits statement III, but the primary deficit of 4,000 crore is correct.
(b) is wrong: it omits statement I, but the revenue deficit of 20,000 crore is correct.
(c) is wrong: it omits statement II, but the fiscal deficit of 10,000 crore, equal to borrowings, is correct.
(d) is right: all three statements (I, II and III) are correct, as the calculations show.
keyfact: Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure - revenue receipts; fiscal deficit = borrowings; primary deficit = fiscal deficit - interest payments.
statements: 1 — Correct: Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure - revenue receipts = 80,000 - 60,000 = 20,000 crore.
2 — Correct: Fiscal deficit equals the government's borrowings, given as 10,000 crore.
3 — Correct: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit - interest payments = 10,000 - 6,000 = 4,000 crore.
summary: The correct answer is (d): all three statements are correct. Revenue deficit = 80,000 - 60,000 = 20,000 crore; fiscal deficit equals total borrowings = 10,000 crore; primary deficit = 10,000 - 6,000 = 4,000 crore.

question: India is one of the founding members of the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), a multimodal transportation corridor, which will connect
options: India to Central Asia to Europe via Iran
India to Central Asia via China
India to South-East Asia through Bangladesh and Myanmar
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The International North-South Transport Corridor was launched by an inter-governmental agreement signed in St Petersburg in September 2000 by India, Iran and Russia. It later expanded to about 13 members, including Azerbaijan, Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkey, Ukraine, Oman, Bulgaria (observer status for some) and Syria. The route runs from Mumbai or Jawaharlal Nehru Port by sea to Bandar Abbas or Chabahar in Iran, then by road and rail across Iran to the Caspian ports such as Bandar Anzali, then across the Caspian or via Azerbaijan by rail to Russia, and onward to Europe. It has three main routes: western (via Azerbaijan), central (trans-Caspian) and eastern (via Central Asia). Its promised benefits are a roughly 30% cost saving and 40% shorter transit than the Suez Canal route. Chabahar port, developed by India, and the Rasht-Astara rail link are key. Elimination: (b) is wrong because the corridor does not pass through China, which is linked to the Belt and Road Initiative. (c) describes the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway and the Bangladesh-linked connectivity, an East-facing route. (d) is incomplete and omits Iran, since Azerbaijan is only a transit link on the western route.
explanations: Correct: the INSTC connects India with Central Asia and Europe via Iran, using Chabahar or Bandar Abbas, the Caspian Sea and Russia.
Incorrect: the INSTC does not go through China. China's connectivity push is the Belt and Road Initiative, which India has opposed over CPEC.
Incorrect: connecting India to South-East Asia via Bangladesh and Myanmar describes eastern projects such as the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway and Kaladan project, not the INSTC.
Incorrect: Azerbaijan is a transit country on the western route, but the corridor's core is the Iran link, so omitting Iran makes this option wrong.
keyfact: INSTC: 2000 St Petersburg agreement (India, Iran, Russia); Mumbai-Bandar Abbas/Chabahar-Caspian-Russia-Europe multimodal route.
summary: The answer is (a): the INSTC is a multimodal (ship, rail, road) route linking India with Central Asia and Europe via Iran. It was designed to cut transit time and cost between the Indian Ocean and the Caspian Sea, Russia and northern Europe.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I : Of the two major ethanol producers in the world, i.e., Brazil and the United States of America, the former produces more ethanol than the latter.
Statement II : Unlike in the United States of America where corn is the principal feedstock for ethanol production, sugarcane is the principal feedstock for ethanol production in Brazil. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement Il explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct
subject: Economy
detail: The US and Brazil together account for roughly 80-85% of global fuel ethanol output. The US produces about 15-16 billion gallons a year (around 55% of world output), almost entirely from corn (maize), in the Corn Belt states such as Iowa, Nebraska and Illinois. Brazil produces about 7-8 billion gallons (around 25-27%), mainly from sugarcane juice and molasses, with a growing share from corn in recent years. Brazil's ethanol programme began with Proalcool in 1975 and was boosted by flex-fuel vehicles from 2003, and Brazil blends about 27% ethanol in petrol. India is the third or fourth largest producer and is pursuing E20 blending, achieved in 2025 under the National Policy on Biofuels 2018, using sugarcane juice, B-heavy molasses, grain and FCI rice. Elimination logic: the question turns on the ranking. Once you know the US leads, Statement I fails, which rules out (a), (b) and (c), because each of them treats Statement I as correct. Only (d) remains, and Statement II is indeed factually accurate.
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement I is incorrect; Brazil does not out-produce the US, so Statement II cannot explain it.
(b) is wrong because Statement I is factually incorrect, even though Statement II is correct.
(c) is wrong because it reverses the truth: Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.
(d) is right because the US is the top ethanol producer (Statement I is false), and the feedstock contrast in Statement II is accurate.
keyfact: The US is the world's No. 1 ethanol producer (corn-based) and Brazil is No. 2 (sugarcane-based).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The US produces more ethanol than Brazil, roughly twice as much, so Brazil is the second largest producer, not the first.
2 — Correct: Corn is the principal feedstock in the US, while sugarcane (juice and molasses) is the principal feedstock in Brazil.
summary: The answer is (d). Statement I is incorrect because the United States, not Brazil, is the world's largest ethanol producer. Statement II is correct because corn is the main feedstock in the US while sugarcane is the main feedstock in Brazil.

question:
The World Bank warned that India could become one of the first places where wet-bulb temperatures routinely exceed 35°C. Which of the following statements best reflect(s) the implication of the above-said report?
I. Peninsular India will most likely suffer from flooding, tropical cyclones and droughts. Il. The survival of animals including humans will be affected as shedding of their body heat through perspiration becomes difficult. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: Wet-bulb temperature is the lowest temperature air can reach by evaporative cooling; it combines heat and humidity. At a wet-bulb temperature of about 35°C (roughly 95°F at 100% humidity), sweat can no longer evaporate from the skin, so a healthy human at rest in shade cannot shed metabolic heat and risks fatal hyperthermia within hours. Mammals and other animals that rely on perspiration or panting face a similar threat, which is why statement II follows directly. The World Bank's 2022 report 'Climate Investment Opportunities in India's Cooling Sector' and related work warn of heat stress, lost labour productivity and cooling demand. The same warming drives an intensified hydrological cycle: more erratic monsoon rainfall, flash floods, stronger tropical cyclones in the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal, and drought spells. Peninsular India, with its long coastline and rain-fed agriculture, is exposed to all of these, so statement I is a reasonable broader implication. Elimination logic: II is clearly right, which removes (a) and (d). I is a plausible climate-linked implication and not contradicted by anything, so (b) is rejected and (c) stands, as the official key confirms.
explanations: (a) is wrong: it omits statement II, which is the most direct physiological implication of wet-bulb temperatures above 35°C.
(b) is wrong: it excludes statement I, but the official key treats climate extremes in peninsular India as a valid implication.
(c) is right: both statements are accepted as implications, one physiological (failure of cooling by perspiration) and one climatic (floods, cyclones, droughts).
(d) is wrong: at least one statement, and in fact both, reflect the implications of the report.
keyfact: A wet-bulb temperature of about 35°C is the human survivability limit because sweat can no longer evaporate to cool the body.
statements: 1 — Correct: Rising temperatures and humidity accompany a more intense climate-change pattern, with floods, cyclones and droughts increasingly likely in peninsular India's coastal and rain-fed regions.
2 — Correct: At a wet-bulb temperature near 35°C, evaporation of sweat fails, so humans and other animals cannot shed body heat, risking heat stroke and death.
summary: The official answer is (c): both statements reflect the implications of the report. Wet-bulb temperatures above 35°C signal extreme heat-humidity stress that blocks the body's cooling by sweating, and they point to a wider pattern of climate extremes (floods, cyclones, droughts) affecting peninsular India.

question: A country’s fiscal deficit stands at €50, 000 crores. It is receiving 10, 000 crores through non-debt creating capital receipts. The country’s interest liabilities are £1, 500 crores. What is the gross primary deficit?
subject: Economy
detail: Gross Fiscal Deficit (GFD) = Total expenditure - (Revenue receipts + Non-debt creating capital receipts). Non-debt creating capital receipts are recovery of loans, disinvestment proceeds and other miscellaneous capital receipts. Since the formula already deducts them, GFD equals the government's net borrowing requirement. If the question gives the fiscal deficit as 50,000 crore, these receipts have already been accounted for and must not be subtracted again. Gross Primary Deficit (GPD) = GFD - interest payments. It shows the government's borrowing need excluding the burden of past debt, so it reflects the current year's fiscal discipline. Here, GPD = 50,000 - 1,500 = 48,500 crore. Related concepts to remember: Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure - Revenue receipts; Effective revenue deficit = Revenue deficit - grants for creation of capital assets; Budgetary deficit is now obsolete. The FRBM Act 2003 set the fiscal deficit target. Elimination logic: 51,500 comes from wrongly adding interest, 58,500 from wrongly adding interest and subtracting the non-debt receipts, and a 'None of the above' answer fails because 48,500 is correct.
explanations: Correct. GPD = GFD - interest = 50,000 - 1,500 = 48,500 crore. The non-debt capital receipts are already included in the fiscal deficit calculation, so they are not subtracted again.
Incorrect. 51,500 results from adding interest liabilities to the fiscal deficit (50,000 + 1,500). The primary deficit is lower than the fiscal deficit, not higher, when interest is positive.
Incorrect. 58,500 would need both adding interest and adding the 10,000 crore, which has no basis. Non-debt receipts are already netted out in the fiscal deficit, so they play no further role.
Incorrect. A valid answer exists among the options, namely 48,500 crore in option (a).
keyfact: Gross primary deficit = Gross fiscal deficit - interest payments; non-debt capital receipts are already deducted in the fiscal deficit.
summary: The answer is (a) ₹48,500 crore. Gross primary deficit = gross fiscal deficit minus interest payments = 50,000 - 1,500 = 48,500 crore. The 10,000 crore of non-debt creating capital receipts is a distractor, because it is already netted out in the fiscal deficit.

question:
Which of the following statements with regard to recommendations of the 15th Finance Commission of India are correct?
I. It has recommended grants of 4, 800 crores from the year 2022-23 to the year 2025-26 for incentivizing States to enhance educational outcomes. Il. 45% of the net proceeds of Union taxes are to be shared with States. Ill. ©45, 000 crores are to be kept as performance-based incentive for all States for carrying out agricultural reforms.
IV. It reintroduced tax effort criteria to reward fiscal performance. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: The 15th Finance Commission was chaired by N.K. Singh and constituted under Article 280. Its report for 2021-26 was tabled in Parliament in February 2021. After Ladakh was separated from the erstwhile J&K state, it kept the states' share of the divisible pool at 41% (42% in the first-year report for 2020-21). This was a small cut from the 14th FC's 42%. The 45% figure is a trap: it is the weight given to the income-distance criterion in the devolution formula. The other weights are population (2011) 15%, area 15%, forest and ecology 10%, demographic performance 12.5%, and tax and fiscal effort 2.5%. The tax effort criterion rewards fiscal performance and was reintroduced by this Commission. The Commission also recommended performance-based incentives: Rs 45,000 crore for agricultural reforms and Rs 4,800 crore for improving educational outcomes over 2022-23 to 2025-26. Since I, III and IV are correct and II is wrong, only option (c) is consistent. Eliminate any option that contains II.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement II, which is false: the states' share is 41%, not 45%.
(b) is wrong because it includes statement II and omits statement III, which is correct.
(c) is correct because I, III and IV are all accurate and II, the only false statement, is excluded.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement II and omits statement I, which is correct.
keyfact: 15th FC: states get 41% of the divisible pool (45% is only the income-distance weight); tax and fiscal effort has a 2.5% weight.
statements: I — Correct: The Commission recommended Rs 4,800 crore for 2022-23 to 2025-26 as incentive grants to states for enhancing educational outcomes.
II — Incorrect: States' share of net proceeds of Union taxes is 41%, not 45%. The 45% figure is the weight of the income-distance criterion.
III — Correct: Rs 45,000 crore was earmarked as a performance-based incentive for states undertaking agricultural reforms.
IV — Correct: Tax and fiscal effort was reintroduced as a devolution criterion with a 2.5% weight, to reward fiscal performance.
summary: The correct answer is (c): statements I, III and IV are correct. Statement II is wrong because the 15th Finance Commission set the states' share of the divisible pool of Union taxes at 41%, not 45%.

question:
Consider the following statements in respect of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) :
I. It provides loans and guarantees to middle income countries.
II. It works single-handedly to help developing countries to reduce poverty.
III. It was established to help Europe rebuild after the World War
II. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: The IBRD was created at the Bretton Woods Conference (July 1944) and began operating in 1946 (the Articles of Agreement came into force in December 1945). It was the first institution of what is now the World Bank Group. Its original mandate was to finance reconstruction of war-devastated Europe; its first loan went to France in 1947. After Europe recovered with the help of the Marshall Plan, it shifted its focus to development in poorer countries. Today it provides loans, guarantees, risk-management products and advisory services to middle-income and creditworthy low-income governments, raising most of its money by issuing bonds in capital markets. The IDA, by contrast, serves the poorest countries with concessional credits and grants. The World Bank Group has five institutions: IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID. The IBRD and IDA together are usually called the World Bank. Its twin goals are ending extreme poverty and boosting shared prosperity. It pursues these with the IMF, UN agencies, regional development banks, governments, the private sector and civil society, so the claim that it works 'single-handedly' is false. Eliminating II removes options (a), (b) and (d), leaving (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong: it includes II, which is incorrect because the IBRD works with partners and not alone.
(b) is wrong: it includes II and leaves out I, which is correct.
(c) is correct: I and III are accurate, and II is the only false statement.
(d) is wrong: it includes statement II, which is false.
keyfact: IBRD: founded at Bretton Woods in 1944 for post-WWII European reconstruction; now lends to middle-income countries and works with partners, not alone.
statements: I — Correct: The IBRD provides loans, guarantees and advisory services mainly to middle-income and creditworthy low-income countries.
II — Incorrect: It does not work single-handedly. It works with the IDA, IFC, MIGA, the IMF, other partners and governments to reduce poverty.
III — Correct: It was established at Bretton Woods (1944) to help rebuild Europe after World War II.
summary: The answer is (c): statements I and III are correct. The IBRD lends to and guarantees for middle-income and creditworthy low-income countries, and it was set up in 1944-45 to finance post-WWII reconstruction of Europe. Statement II is wrong because the IBRD does not work single-handedly; it works as part of the World Bank Group and with partners.

question:
Consider the following statements in respect of RTGS and NEFT :
I. In RTGS, the settlement time is instantaneous while in case of NEFT, it takes some time to settle payments. Il. In RTGS, the customer is charged for inward transactions while that is not the case for NEFT. Ill. Operating hours for RTGS are restricted on certain days while this is not true for NEFT. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement) and NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer) are RBI-operated retail and large-value payment systems. RTGS settles each transaction individually and continuously on a gross basis in central bank money, so funds move instantaneously and the transfer is final and irrevocable. It is meant for large-value transfers, with a minimum of Rs 2 lakh. NEFT works on Deferred Net Settlement in half-hourly batches, so there is a delay of some time before settlement. It has no minimum or maximum limit. Since December 2019 NEFT has operated 24x7x365, and RTGS has also run 24x7 since December 2020, so neither has restricted hours on certain days. That makes Statement III incorrect. RBI had also directed that no charges be levied on inward transactions, meaning receipt of funds, for either RTGS or NEFT. Customers are not charged for inward credits in either system, so Statement II is incorrect. Elimination logic: once II is spotted as false, options (b) is out. Once III is identified as false, (c) and (d) are out, leaving (a).
explanations: (a) is right: only Statement I is correct, as RTGS is real-time gross settlement and NEFT is batch-based.
(b) is wrong: it includes Statement II, but inward transactions are free for both RTGS and NEFT.
(c) is wrong: it includes Statement III, but both systems operate 24x7 on all days, so RTGS hours are not restricted.
(d) is wrong: Statement III is incorrect and it also leaves out the correct Statement I.
keyfact: RTGS = real-time gross settlement (min Rs 2 lakh); NEFT = batch-based deferred net settlement; both are 24x7 and have no inward charges.
statements: 1 — Correct: RTGS gives real-time, gross, immediate and final settlement, whereas NEFT settles in periodic batches (deferred net settlement), hence takes some time.
2 — Incorrect: Inward transactions are not charged for either RTGS or NEFT; the beneficiary customer pays nothing for receiving funds.
3 — Incorrect: Both systems are available round the clock on all days (NEFT since Dec 2019, RTGS since Dec 2020), so neither has restricted hours on certain days.
summary: The answer is (a): only Statement I is correct. RTGS settles payments individually and in real time (gross settlement), whereas NEFT settles in batches, so it takes some time. Statements II and III are factually wrong about charges and operating hours.

question:
Consider the following countries :
I. United Arab Emirates Il, France Ill. Germany
IV. Singapore
V. Bangladesh How many countries amongst the above are there other than India where international merchant payments are accepted under UPI?
subject: Economy
detail: UPI (Unified Payments Interface) is run by NPCI, and its international arm, NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL), signs agreements with foreign payment networks to enable UPI acceptance abroad. Singapore was the first major linkage: UPI-PayNow, launched in February 2023, a person-to-person remittance link between UPI and Singapore's PayNow, with UPI QR merchant acceptance also available through NETS. In the UAE, UPI acceptance was enabled through Network International's terminals, with the agreement signed in 2024. France became the first European country to accept UPI when it launched at the Eiffel Tower in February 2024, through Lyra. Other countries where UPI is live include Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Mauritius. Germany and Bangladesh are not on this list of merchant-payment countries, so they must be eliminated. That leaves exactly three of the five: UAE, France and Singapore. Hence (b). Students should distinguish between UPI merchant payments (QR-based acceptance) and remittance or P2P linkages, since the question asks specifically about merchant payments.
explanations: (a) Only two is wrong: the count is three, since the UAE, France and Singapore all accept UPI merchant payments.
(b) Only three is right: the UAE, France and Singapore accept UPI merchant payments, while Germany and Bangladesh do not.
(c) Only four is wrong: it would require Germany or Bangladesh to also accept UPI merchant payments, which they do not.
(d) All the five is wrong: Germany and Bangladesh are not on the list of countries accepting UPI merchant payments.
keyfact: UPI merchant payments abroad: UAE, France (Eiffel Tower, 2024) and Singapore, but not Germany or Bangladesh.
statements: 1 — Correct: UAE accepts UPI merchant payments through Network International's terminals, enabled through an NIPL agreement.
2 — Correct: France accepts UPI merchant payments, launched at the Eiffel Tower in 2024 through Lyra, the first European country to do so.
3 — Incorrect: Germany is not among the countries where UPI merchant payments are accepted.
4 — Correct: Singapore accepts UPI QR merchant payments through NETS, and also has the UPI-PayNow remittance link.
5 — Incorrect: Bangladesh is not among the countries where UPI merchant payments are accepted.
summary: The official answer is (b) Only three. Of the five countries listed, UPI merchant payments are accepted in the UAE, France and Singapore, while Germany and Bangladesh are not on the list of countries where UPI is accepted for merchant payments.

question:
Consider the following statements about PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana’ :
I. It targets installation of one crore solar rooftop panels in the residential sector. Il. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy aims to impart training on installation, operation, maintenance and repairs of solar rooftop systems at grassroot levels. Ill. It aims to create more than three lakhs skilled manpower through fresh skilling, and upskilling, under scheme component of capacity building. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana was announced by the Prime Minister in February 2024 and approved by the Union Cabinet on 29 February 2024, with an outlay of about Rs 75,021 crore, to be implemented up to FY 2026-27. The nodal ministry is the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE). The objective is to install rooftop solar in one crore residential households, giving up to 300 units of free electricity per month. The scheme gives Central Financial Assistance (CFA) of about 60% of the cost for systems up to 2 kW and 40% for the additional capacity up to 3 kW, with a cap on the subsidy. It also offers collateralised-free low-interest loans. Households apply through the national portal. The scheme includes components for capacity building, awareness and outreach, and for skilling. Under this, MNRE aims to train people in installation, operation, maintenance and repair of rooftop systems at the grassroots level, and to create more than three lakh skilled professionals through fresh skilling and upskilling. This includes solar installers, technicians and related roles. It also promotes model solar villages and encourages local bodies to adopt rooftop solar. Since statements I, II and III all match the scheme's official objectives, the only option that includes all three is (d). Options (a), (b) and (c) each wrongly exclude a correct statement.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it omits statement III, which is also correct.
(b) is wrong because it omits statement II, which is also correct.
(c) is wrong because it omits statement I, which is also correct.
(d) is correct because statements I, II and III all accurately describe the scheme.
keyfact: PM Surya Ghar (Feb 2024, MNRE): 1 crore households rooftop solar, up to 300 free units a month, Rs 75,021 crore outlay, plus capacity building to create over 3 lakh skilled workers.
statements: I — Correct: The scheme targets rooftop solar installation in one crore residential households.
II — Correct: MNRE aims to provide grassroots training in installation, operation, maintenance and repair of rooftop solar systems as part of the scheme's capacity-building and skilling effort.
III — Correct: The capacity-building component aims to create over three lakh skilled personnel through fresh skilling and upskilling.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana targets one crore households with rooftop solar, and its capacity-building component covers grassroots training and creation of a large skilled workforce.

question: “Sedition has become my religion” was the famous statement given by Gandhiji at the time of the Champaran Satyagraha
options: publicly violating Salt Law at Dandi
Conference in London the launch of the Quit India
subject: Modern History
detail: The Salt March (Dandi March) began on 12 March 1930 from Sabarmati Ashram with 78 followers. It ended at Dandi on 6 April 1930, when Gandhi broke the salt law by picking up natural salt. This launched the Civil Disobedience Movement, the first big mass movement after Non-Cooperation. Gandhi had already issued the 11-point demands to Viceroy Irwin, who ignored them. The salt tax was chosen because it hit every Indian, especially the poor. Gandhi's statement that sedition had become his religion reflects his view that a government he considered immoral deserved open, non-violent defiance. It also echoes his 1922 trial, where he called Section 124A (sedition) the 'prince among the political sections of the IPC designed to suppress the liberty of the citizen'. Elimination logic: Champaran (1917) was about the indigo tinkathia system and was a movement for peasants' rights. It was not an act of defying law as a creed. The Second Round Table Conference (1931) followed the Gandhi-Irwin Pact and was a negotiation. Quit India (1942) is associated with 'Do or Die'.
explanations: (a) Incorrect as the answer to this question: at Champaran (1917) Gandhi's focus was the tinkathia indigo system and peasant grievances, and his famous words there were not 'sedition is my religion'. Note that the OCR scrambled the options, so this is just the first listed option.

(b) Correct: the statement is linked to the Salt Satyagraha of 1930, when Gandhi publicly broke the salt law at Dandi and launched Civil Disobedience, treating defiance of the unjust law as a moral duty.

(c) Incorrect: the Second Round Table Conference (September to December 1931) was a negotiation, and Gandhi attended it as the sole Congress representative after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact. It was not an act of defiance.
(d) Incorrect: the Quit India Movement (August 1942) is associated with the slogan 'Do or Die' and the Gowalia Tank speech, not this statement.
keyfact: 'Sedition has become my religion' is linked to the 1930 Salt Satyagraha (Dandi, 6 April 1930), the start of Civil Disobedience.
summary: The answer is (b), publicly violating the Salt Law at Dandi. In 1930 Gandhi said 'Sedition has become my religion' to show that open defiance of an unjust colonial state was now a moral duty. The remark belongs to the Civil Disobedience Movement.

ocr: The famous female figurine known as Dancing Girl’, found at Mohenjo-daro, is made of carnelian (a) (b) clay bronze (c) gold (a)
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Dancing Girl was discovered at Mohenjo-daro (Sindh, now in Pakistan) in 1926 by the archaeologist Ernest Mackay. It is about 10.5 cm tall and shows a nude young woman in a confident, relaxed pose, with one hand on the hip and an arm covered in bangles. She wears a necklace and her hair is tied in a bun. It is a bronze figurine, cast by the lost-wax (cire perdue) process. In this method a wax model is coated in clay, the wax is melted out, and molten metal is poured into the mould. This shows that Harappans mastered copper-tin alloying. Other well-known bronze objects of the civilisation include the bronze bull and the bronze bullock cart from Chanhudaro/Harappa. The Priest-King bust, by contrast, is made of steatite. Terracotta figures such as the Mother Goddess are clay, while carnelian was used for beads, famously from Chanhudaro. Gold was used for ornaments, not for this figurine. Elimination: the question refers to a famous metal figurine, which rules out clay and carnelian. Gold is rare and used for jewellery, so bronze is the answer.
explanations: Incorrect: carnelian is a semi-precious stone used by the Harappans for beads and ornaments, not for sculpting figurines such as the Dancing Girl.
Incorrect: clay (terracotta) was used for Mother Goddess figurines, toys and animal figures, but the Dancing Girl is a metal casting, not a clay object.
Correct: the Dancing Girl is a bronze statuette made by the lost-wax technique, which shows Harappan skill in metallurgy.
Incorrect: gold was used for jewellery and small ornaments in the Indus cities, not for this statuette, which is bronze.
keyfact: Dancing Girl (Mohenjo-daro, found 1926 by Mackay) = bronze, lost-wax casting; Priest-King = steatite.
summary: The correct answer is (c) bronze. The 'Dancing Girl' of Mohenjo-daro is a small bronze statuette made by the lost-wax (cire perdue) technique, which shows the advanced metallurgy of the Harappans.

ocr: Who provided legal defence to the people arrested in the aftermath of Chauri Chaura incident? Cc. R. Das (a) Madan Mohan Malaviya and (b) Krishna Kant Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Khwaja (c) Hasan Nizami M. A. Jinnah (d)
subject: Current Affairs
detail: On 4 February 1922, a mob of peasants and Non-Cooperation volunteers at Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur district, United Provinces) set fire to a police station, killing 22-23 policemen, after police fired on a procession. Gandhi, shocked by the violence, suspended the Non-Cooperation Movement on 12 February 1922 (the Bardoli decision). The Sessions Court at Gorakhpur sentenced 172 accused to death. Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya, a lawyer and Congress leader who had left the legal profession decades earlier, returned to the court to argue the appeal before the Allahabad High Court. As a result, the High Court (1923) upheld death sentences for 19 and commuted many others to life imprisonment or shorter terms; the majority of the 172 were saved. Malaviya's role is a classic UPSC fact, linked to his later founding of Banaras Hindu University (1916) and his Congress presidency. Elimination logic: C. R. Das defended Aurobindo Ghose in the Alipore Bomb case (1908), not Chauri Chaura. Kitchlew and Khwaja Hasan Nizami were linked to the Khilafat and Punjab events, and Jinnah had distanced himself from Congress non-cooperation, so options (c) and (d) do not fit.
explanations: (a) Incorrect: C. R. Das is famous for defending Aurobindo Ghose in the Alipore Bomb Case (1908) and for founding the Swaraj Party in 1923, not for the Chauri Chaura defence.

(b) Correct: Madan Mohan Malaviya, with Krishna Kant, organised and conducted the defence of the accused; of the 172 sentenced to death by the Gorakhpur court, most were saved on appeal in the Allahabad High Court.

(c) Incorrect: Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew was a Punjab Congress and Khilafat leader associated with the Jallianwala Bagh agitation, and Khwaja Hasan Nizami was a Sufi writer and Khilafat supporter; neither is linked to the Chauri Chaura defence.
(d) Incorrect: M. A. Jinnah had left the Congress in 1920 over non-cooperation and was not involved in defending the Chauri Chaura accused; he is better known for defending Tilak in 1916.
keyfact: Chauri Chaura (4 Feb 1922): Madan Mohan Malaviya defended the accused, saving most of the 172 sentenced to death; Gandhi suspended Non-Cooperation on 12 Feb 1922.
summary: The answer is (b) Madan Mohan Malaviya and Krishna Kant. After the Chauri Chaura incident of 4 February 1922, Malaviya led the legal defence of the accused, which saved many of them from the gallows. He was assisted by lawyers such as Krishna Kant Malaviya.

question: Subsequent to which one of the following events, Gandhiji, who consistently opposed untouchability and appealed for its eradication from all spheres, decided to include the upliftment of ‘Harijans’ in his political and social programme?
options: Arrest of Congress leadership at the time of the Quit India Movement
Promulgation of the Government of India Act, 1935
subject: Modern History
detail: Gandhi had condemned untouchability since his South Africa days, but it became an organised mission after the Poona Pact. The Communal Award of Ramsay MacDonald (16 August 1932) provided separate electorates for the Depressed Classes. Gandhi, then in Yerwada Jail, began a fast unto death on 20 September 1932 against this. Talks between Gandhi's side (Madan Mohan Malaviya, Rajendra Prasad and others) and B.R. Ambedkar led to the Poona Pact on 24 September 1932. It replaced separate electorates with reserved seats within general electorates, raising the reserved seats for the Depressed Classes in provincial legislatures from 71 to 147 and providing 18% of central legislature seats. Soon afterwards Gandhi founded the All India Anti-Untouchability League (September 1932), later renamed the Harijan Sevak Sangh. He launched the weekly Harijan (February 1933) and undertook the Harijan Yatra tour in 1933-34. Elimination logic: the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931) dealt with suspending civil disobedience and releasing prisoners, with no link to Harijans. The Government of India Act 1935 came after the Harijan campaign had begun. The Quit India arrests (1942) came a decade later and concerned independence.
explanations: Correct: the Poona Pact of September 1932 ended Gandhi's fast over separate electorates, and he then launched the Harijan Sevak Sangh and the Harijan campaign as part of his programme.
Incorrect: the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931 concerned suspension of civil disobedience, release of prisoners and participation in the Second Round Table Conference, not Harijan upliftment.
Incorrect: the Quit India arrests of August 1942 came about ten years after Gandhi's Harijan campaign began, and that movement concerned ending British rule.

Incorrect: the Government of India Act 1935 followed the Poona Pact and the start of the Harijan campaign, so it could not have prompted the decision; it did provide for Scheduled Castes representation.
keyfact: Poona Pact (24 Sept 1932) led to Gandhi's Harijan Sevak Sangh and the weekly Harijan (1933).
summary: The answer is (a) The Poona Pact. After the Communal Award (August 1932) gave Depressed Classes separate electorates, Gandhi's fast unto death in Yerwada Jail ended with the Poona Pact (24 September 1932). He then made Harijan upliftment a central part of his political and social programme.

question:
Consider the following fruits :
I. Papaya Il. Pineapple Ill. Guava How many of the above were introduced in India by the Portuguese in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This question tests the Columbian Exchange and the Portuguese role in India's agriculture. After Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 and the Portuguese made Goa their base (captured 1510 under Afonso de Albuquerque), they brought many American crops to India. Papaya (native to Central America and Mexico), pineapple (South America, Brazil-Paraguay region) and guava (tropical America) arrived via Goa and the west coast in the 1500s and 1600s. Other Portuguese-introduced crops that UPSC likes to ask about include potato, tomato, maize, chilli, groundnut, cashew, tobacco, custard apple, sweet potato and sapota (chikoo). Tobacco is a classic: it came in Akbar's time, reportedly through the Portuguese, and Jahangir tried to ban it. Elimination logic: all three are non-native American fruits, which makes (d) None and (a) or (b) unlikely. Native Indian fruits such as mango, jackfruit, banana, jamun and citrus were not introduced by Europeans. Recognising that the three fruits share a New World origin is enough to answer correctly: if you know one is a Portuguese introduction, the shared origin suggests the others are too.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Not just one fruit; all three were introduced by the Portuguese.
(b) Wrong: Not just two; the third is also a Portuguese introduction from the New World.
(c) Correct: Papaya, pineapple and guava were all introduced by the Portuguese via Goa and the west coast in the 16th-17th centuries.
(d) Wrong: At least one, in fact all three, were introduced by the Portuguese, so 'none' is false.
keyfact: Portuguese (via Goa) brought New World crops to India: papaya, pineapple, guava, potato, tomato, maize, chilli, groundnut, cashew, tobacco.
statements: 1 — Correct: Papaya is native to tropical America and was introduced to India by the Portuguese in the 16th-17th centuries.
2 — Correct: Pineapple is native to South America and was brought to India by the Portuguese in the 16th century.
3 — Correct: Guava is native to tropical America and was introduced to India by the Portuguese in the 16th-17th centuries.
summary: The answer is (c) All the three. Papaya, pineapple and guava are all New World fruits brought to India by the Portuguese in the 16th-17th centuries, after Columbus's voyages opened the Columbian Exchange.

question:
Consider the following countries :
I. United Kingdom Il. Denmark Ill. New Zealand
IV. Australia Vv. Brazil How many of the above countries have more than four time zones?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question counts all time zones a country uses, including those of its overseas and dependent territories. The United Kingdom has about nine, running from Pitcairn (UTC-8) to the British Indian Ocean Territory (UTC+6), covering the Falklands, Gibraltar, Cayman Islands, Bermuda, St Helena and others. Denmark spans several through Greenland (roughly UTC-4 to UTC+0, including Danmarkshavn and Thule), the Faroe Islands (UTC+0) and mainland Denmark (UTC+1). New Zealand has mainland NZST (UTC+12), the Chatham Islands (+12:45), Tokelau (+13), and Niue (-11) and the Cook Islands (-10), which are self-governing states in free association with New Zealand. Australia has three mainland zones (AWST +8, ACST +9:30, AEST +10), plus Lord Howe Island (+10:30), Christmas Island (+7), Cocos Islands (+6:30) and Norfolk Island (+11). Brazil, despite its size, has only four (UTC-2 Fernando de Noronha, -3 Brasília, -4 Amazonas, -5 Acre), so it is not 'more than four'. Hence four countries qualify. Elimination: Brazil is a classic trap for 'big country, many zones', which rules out (a).
explanations: (a) is wrong because Brazil has only four time zones (UTC-2 to -5), so not all five qualify.
(b) is correct because the UK, Denmark, New Zealand and Australia each have more than four time zones, and Brazil does not.
(c) is wrong because it undercounts. Denmark (via Greenland) and New Zealand (via its Pacific territories) also exceed four, so three is too few.
(d) is wrong because far more than two countries qualify. Four of the five do.
keyfact: Count overseas territories: the UK (~9), Denmark, New Zealand and Australia have more than four time zones, but Brazil has exactly four.
statements: I — Correct: the UK has about nine time zones, counting its overseas territories.
II — Correct: Denmark has more than four zones when Greenland and the Faroe Islands are included.
III — Correct: New Zealand has five or more, counting Chatham, Tokelau, the Cook Islands and Niue.
IV — Correct: Australia has more than four, counting three mainland zones plus Lord Howe, Christmas, Cocos and Norfolk islands.
V — Incorrect: Brazil has exactly four time zones, which is not more than four.
summary: The answer is (b): only four of the five countries have more than four time zones. The United Kingdom, Denmark, New Zealand and Australia exceed four once overseas territories are counted, while Brazil has exactly four.

ocr: Consider the following statements : I. Anadyr in Siberia and Nome in Alaska are a few kilometers from each other, but when people are waking up and getting set for breakfast in these cities, it would be different days. Il. When it is Monday in Anadyr, it is Tuesday in Nome. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) I only (b) I only (c) Both I and II (a) Neither I nor II
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The International Date Line (IDL) runs roughly along the 180° meridian, deviating around the Bering Strait, Aleutian Islands, Fiji, Kiribati and Tonga so that political units keep the same date. Crossing it from west to east (for example Asia to North America) you subtract a day; crossing east to west you add a day. Anadyr in Chukotka (Russia) uses UTC+12, while Nome in Alaska uses UTC-9 (UTC-8 in daylight time), so the gap is about 21 hours (20 in summer). The two places are only a few hundred kilometres apart across the Bering Strait, yet fall on opposite sides of the Date Line, so at breakfast time they are normally on different calendar days. The place west of the line (Anadyr) is ahead in time because the Earth rotates west to east, so it sees the sun first. Hence Anadyr is always the 'later' date: Monday in Anadyr means Sunday in Nome. Elimination: Statement I is a well-known fact about the Date Line, so (b) and (c) go out. Statement II reverses the direction of the date change, so it is wrong, which rules out (c) and (d) as well and leaves (a).
explanations: (a) Correct: Statement I is true and Statement II is false because the direction of the date difference is reversed.
(b) Wrong: Statement II is false, since Nome is behind Anadyr, so Monday in Anadyr is Sunday in Nome.
(c) Wrong: It includes Statement II, which is incorrect.
(d) Wrong: Statement I is correct, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: West of the International Date Line is a day ahead: Monday in Anadyr (Russia) is Sunday in Nome (Alaska).
statements: 1 — Correct: Anadyr and Nome are close across the Bering Strait but lie on opposite sides of the International Date Line, so at the same moment they usually have different calendar dates (about 20-21 hours apart).
2 — Incorrect: Anadyr, west of the Date Line, is ahead of Nome. When it is Monday in Anadyr it is Sunday in Nome, not Tuesday.
summary: The answer is (a): only Statement I is correct. Anadyr (Russia) and Nome (Alaska, USA) lie very close across the Bering Strait but on opposite sides of the International Date Line, so their calendar dates differ. Anadyr is ahead of Nome, however, so when it is Monday in Anadyr it is Sunday in Nome, not Tuesday.

question: Who among the following was the founder of the ‘Self-Respect Movement’?
subject: Current Affairs
